utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Dr. Michael Williams. Your Honour, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder of 42 exhibits. Could I ask that a number be assigned at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the large number of exhibits and in the interest of expediting the proceedings here this morning, I'm going to ask, with the Court's permission, that Dr. Williams be allowed to have the same copy of exhibits that we all have and that he can simply turn to the tab and comment appropriately on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, could I ask you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Michael Charles Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we begin by showing you Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 1. If you would flip to the first tab of your binder. Do you recognise what that document is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter from Mr. Vieira de Mello to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm going to ask that you be shown this document. It wasn't included in your binder last evening.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I do recognise this. It's my curriculum vitae of my professional career.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does that accurately record your educational and professional accomplishments?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It does. And I'm currently special advisor to the Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 2, and ask you do you recognise this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the usher would be so kind as to show this particular one, and then the rest of the exhibits are included in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise what Prosecution tab 2, 470 is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's a summary table of the exhibits that have been reviewed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do the comments in the right-hand column of that exhibit accurately reflect your comments regarding the context and other information regarding the exhibits that you reviewed and will be speaking to this morning?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now ask you to describe your connections with the former Yugoslavia. During what period of time were you employed in work there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I went to the former Yugoslavia in February 1994. Previously, I'd served with the United Nations mission in Cambodia as deputy director of human rights. The head of that mission, Mr. Akashi, then asked me to accompany him to the former Yugoslavia, where I assumed the post of director of information in February 1994, a post I held until the middle of April, April the 17th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe your duty -- your duties and your authority in that post.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My duties were varied. I was one of a small group of senior officials that advised Mr. Akashi on general policy. I was his senior spokesman for the region, and I was director of the information component which tried, as accurately as possible, to relay the unfolding of events within the region both to the inhabitants of that region and to the wider international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of your tenure in this position, did you attend regularly scheduled or daily meetings with Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Every day the normal procedure would be that the senior staff meeting would take place in the headquarters in Zagreb at 8.30 for approximately 60 minutes six days a week, Monday to Saturday. If, as alas was frequently the case, due to the urgency of events on the ground, there were also meetings on Sunday, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe not so much the names of the people but what organisations were represented at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were roughly about 20 people attending the meeting, both civilians and military officials. It would always include the force commander, the head of the military force of the UN protection force, which in my time was a French general, General Bertrand de Lapresle. There would also be other senior military and civilian officials, including representatives of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your post, did you have access to all of the reporting that Mr. Akashi would have seen in execution of his responsibilities as special advisor?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw all classified material and code cables, both reports from military and civilian officials in the field, in Croatia, in Bosnia, as well as our offices in Belgrade, and the coded cables that went in and out from Zagreb to United Nations headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you to just to comment more specifically on your relationship with representatives of UNHCR. And can you put it, please, in the context of the situation in the Republika Srpska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had a close relationship with them. Much of my professional career has been in the humanitarian field, in human rights. I've worked in the past for organisations like Amnesty International, and indeed my responsibilities, as I alluded earlier, in Cambodia were wholly in the field of human rights. With regard to the Republika Srpska, the whole time that I was in the former Yugoslavia, and indeed the period before that, from 1992 onwards, it caused me great concern that the international community, the UN agencies, did not have proper access to the Republika Srpska, that they were unable to fulfil and to properly carry out their mandates. UNHCR did have limited access, and because of that I was particularly close to a number of officials in order to try and apprise myself as best as possible of the situation pertaining in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've said that UN officials did not have proper access. Leaving aside for the moment the representatives of UNHCR, what in fact was the access that UN officials had to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, there could be a short answer to that, which would virtually be none. Mr. Akashi continually asked that he be allowed to visit Banja Luka and other parts of Republika Srpska; Banja Luka, because it's the largest city in the Republika Srpska, but also because still at this time it contained quite considerable numbers of minority communities, both Muslims and Croats, and smaller numbers of Romanies. The information that we were receiving was that the condition of these communities was quite desperate. Despite his pleas, Mr. Akashi was never on a single occasion allowed to visit Republika Srpska. It did not stop there; and all other senior UN officials were not allowed to visit. I think it's also relevant to the Court that members of the international press corps were not allowed to visit the Republika Srpska. I think if -- if I may, in some respect, the authorities in the Republika Srpska learnt perhaps a lesson from the almost accidental discovery by foreign correspondents of the camps at Omarska and Trnopolje in late 1992. Following those events, it was nigh on impossible for foreign correspondents to visit the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, can I ask you to briefly describe what, if any, relationship you had with members of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had a relationship with them. As the Court will be aware, the International Committee of the Red Cross has a long-standing responsibility to carry out its humanitarian duties in situations of warfare, both warfare between states and warfare within states. In that respect, throughout the former Yugoslavia it continued to function, even in the difficulties that prevailed in those years. Where possible I did try and meet with officials of the Red Cross, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, your comments regarding the limited access that international -- the international community had to the Republika Srpska, did that also include the enclaves of Muslim community in Bosnia, particularly Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And I think this is a particularly -- a particularly awful aspect of the UN mission, if I may say so, that access to the three eastern zones, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa, was out of the question. Mr. Akashi never visited any of those enclaves. It was made clear by the Bosnian Serb authorities that a visit to those enclaves would be unwelcome, despite the -- despite the fact that these were enclaves of the Bosnian government, a government recognised by the United Nations, and moreover these enclaves were declared safe havens under resolutions 824 and 836 of the Security Council. I should also add that it was not just Mr. Akashi in this regard. Other senior officials were prevented from visiting the enclaves. I once personally requested Dr. Karadzic for permission to visit the enclaves, and that was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when it was possible to have at least one civilian representative of UNPROFOR enter the enclave of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The head of civil affairs, Mr. Vieira de Mello, went into Gorazde in late April 1994 with the first convoy to reach the besieged enclave following the -- the concerted Serb assault on that enclave in April. Later that year I also ensured that one of my most senior human rights officers who had worked with me in Cambodia was appointed -- sent to Gorazde as a senior UN representative there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was Mr. Craig Jenness of Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will ask you in detail later in your testimony about the humanitarian situation. But could I ask you at this time to summarise the humanitarian situation in Republika Srpska, in particular the enclaves, as you found it during your tenure in your post?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think one has to distinguish between the enclaves and the Republika Srpska. With regard to the Republika Srpska, I think the humanitarian situation in the 15 months or so that I was present was dire. This fluctuated, obviously, dependent upon the access that the UN and UNHCR had to the enclaves. Unlike Sarajevo, where there was the possibility of air access, the eastern enclaves could only be accessed by road, and those roads were controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities. There were periods, obviously, when convoys carrying humanitarian supplies - food, medicines, and so on - did get through, but there were very, very long periods, particularly from late 1994 onwards and in the first six months of 1995 when access was almost impossible. I remember Mr. Akashi in one of his strongest letters to Dr. Radovan Karadzic expressed, in his words, utter dismay at the absence of any medical supplies, any meaningful medical supplies, in the enclaves, including -- and absence of antibiotics, anti-cardiac drugs, and even medicines as basic as aspirin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it possible for people that were critically ill in the enclaves to be medevaced out of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: With rare exception, no. There were some medical evacuations following the limited abatement of the crisis around Gorazde in late April 1994, but I'll give an indication perhaps of how difficult the situation had become by early 1995. My own, as it were, representative in Gorazde, Craig Jenness, was himself refused access to leave the enclave by the Bosnian Serbs for a period of three months. Now, if these were conditions that were placed upon an international official, it goes without saying that an ordinary citizen and resident of the enclaves had a pitiful chance of -- of being allowed out even for medical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were personally involved in an attempt to medevac two very seriously injured British soldiers who were military observers in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I was personally involved in this sense: I was in the headquarters in Zagreb on that day. The day would have been Friday, April the 15th, 1994. The British soldiers were members of an SAS unit that had entered Gorazde some, I think, a week -- eight or nine days earlier. Two of these soldiers were at an observation post which came under concerted fire from Bosnian Serb forces, including machine-gun and mortar fire. My recollection of the timing is that at -- Mr. Akashi, who was that day in Pale, the Bosnian Serb headquarters, talking to Dr. Karadzic, was informed at 17.53 that two of the soldiers had been hit and were seriously injured. There then followed harrowing negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs to see if a helicopter would be allowed to approach Gorazde to evacuate the two soldiers. One of the soldiers had sustained very heavy injuries. Eventually at 8.00 it was able to move -- the two soldiers were able to move to Gorazde hospital, where they were then -- which had very, very limited facilities, by the way. And they were then subsequently taken by helicopter to Sarajevo, where they arrived at 10.00, I think almost four and a half hours after the incident in which they were shot, and alas, one of the soldiers died very soon after his arrival in Sarajevo from his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, if I can draw your attention now to another subject. Did you in the course of your duties attend meetings with Mr. Akashi with senior members of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did, very frequently. These meetings usually took place in Pale, the Bosnian Serb republic. They were usually quite extensive meetings, I think almost always on a Friday, usually starting in late afternoon and continuing up until midnight. There was at least one occasion when I went to Pale on my own to meet with Dr. Karadzic and there was also an occasion in June 1994, the first week of June 1994, when I accompanied Mr. Akashi in negotiations that were held with the Bosnian Serbs and also the Bosnian government leadership in Geneva, negotiations to try and bring about a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to identify some of the more senior members of the Bosnian Serb delegation, including military leaders, that would attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: General Mladic was also present, in my recollection. He might often be accompanied by other Bosnian Serb military leaders, General Gvero was one who was frequently present. On the civil leadership, it was usually quite a large gathering. It was one of the -- I always found that actually rather unusual in some respects, that as many as eight or nine civilian leaders would be present. Those always present, I think, were Dr. Karadzic himself; Mr. Krajisnik, speaker of the Bosnian Serb parliamentary assembly; Alex Buha, the Foreign Minister; Professor Koljevic, the vice-president; General Tolimir was also sometimes present. Those are the names I recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of these meetings, did you form an opinion with respect to Mr. -- General Mladic's ability or the -- the structural command of the Army of Republika Srpska, the effectiveness of that command structure?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My assessment, both from the meetings I attended in which he was -- was present and also my assessment from the reports that I -- we received from the field and from my own reading, was that it was a fairly disciplined military structure and that he was a firm and decisive commander. Its structure, of course, bears the hallmarks of its origins, namely that this came from and still held close links with the old JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, subsequently the JA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there ever a concrete example where General Mladic was able to pick up the phone or pick up some kind of communication device and communicate an order that you knew was observed a short time later?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a very striking example when we were in Geneva. I referred earlier to the Gorazde crisis, which took place in April 1994. That crisis, alas, like so many of the crises in Bosnia, never satisfactorily resolved itself. As part of the agreement reached in Belgrade on April the 22nd and April the 23rd, 1994, the Bosnian Serb forces were supposed to withdraw from a 3-kilometre zone around the centre of the city. Now, that withdrawal was never complete. When we were in Geneva, we found out from the Bosnian government that some Bosnian Serb forces remained within that zone. Dr. Karadzic was very unwilling to make any efforts on this, and Mr. Akashi warned him that talks could not proceed whilst they were still violating the zone and violating an agreement reached in Belgrade. Karadzic blamed it on the Muslims. He said, "The Muslims will always try and make trouble." Mladic, who was more withdrawn in the discussion, then involved himself and said, "Leave this to me." He subsequently spoke with his force commander, I would guess, in the area and those forces left the zone within 24 hours, enabling the talks to take place in Geneva. I should say that the particular Bosnian Serb unit was actually in a difficult situation. I think it was on an -- a fairly isolated ridge which was difficult to evacuate in a short period of time. But I think it's an indication of the -- the way the command structure was intact throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Williams, during the course of these meetings, would the Bosnian Serb leadership and, in fact, General Mladic be made aware of the humanitarian situation and other important issues that the United Nations delegation felt important to bring to their attention?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, continually. I couldn't think of a single meeting where the humanitarian situation was not brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, I'm going to ask you to turn to tab 3. And it will also be displayed on the TV monitors on the Sanction system. And I'm going to ask you just to summarise or comment on this document. And is this document an example of Dr. Karadzic being advised of crimes being committed or the intentional targeting and destruction of civilian homes by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's a letter, as you see, from the head of civil affairs, Mr. de Mello, to Dr. Karadzic, citing specific instances with grid references and so on, in which Bosnian forces in a number of areas in North-Western Bosnia, a number of villages, deliberately civilian houses, knowing full well that in many cases, as he points out, these houses were still occupied. Mr. de Mello goes on to draw the attention of Dr. Karadzic to some of the relevant provisions of the Geneva Conventions with regard to international humanitarian law, even in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in this letter, dated the 3rd of March, 1994, are some of the locations include Bosanska Krupa, Otoko, Dornja, Pokoj, and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct. I would say this letter was substantial of quite a number of either Mr. de Mello or Mr. Akashi himself wrote to Dr. Karadzic in the 15 or 16 months I was in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Williams, I'd like to draw your attention to a completely different subject, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it written only on English? If you could help me. Was it not translated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been written, Your Honour, only in -- in English. Dr. Karadzic spoke very excellent English and had no difficulty in reading documents in English. And quite a number of the other Bosnian Serb leaders also spoke and read good English, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to the period of time after the failure of the Vance-Owen Plan to be adopted by the Assembly of Republika Srpska. Can I ask you to describe your observations of the relationship between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Serb leadership at that time or during that period.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the relationship became strained; that was clear, both after the failure of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan but also in 1994, after the failure of the contact group peace plan. And it was at that juncture that, for example, Mr. Milosevic, then president of the Serbia, announced sanctions against the Bosnian Serb leadership and against the Republika Srpska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 5 and draw your attention to the second page. I'm going to read a sentence from the bottom paragraph and ask you to put this in context for us. The sentence reads: "A delegation of the members of the assembly led by 'Foreign Minister' Buha and including the leader of the SDS deputies in the Assembly v. Maksimovic visited Belgrade and met with Milosevic. The visit coincided with the statement by SDS executive board condemning 'unauthorised visits and meetings' of members of the Bosnian Serb to Belgrade and for a time caused a certain confusion as to the actual support Buha's mission enjoyed at Pale." Can I ask you to place that in context and comment on it for us.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're having difficulty finding it, perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, no, I've found it now. Sorry. My fault. Yes, this document dates from December 1994. I'm sorry, Mr. Groome, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question is: Can you put this in context. Was there confusion from the UN delegation regarding what the public stance was regarding the relationship, as opposed to what appeared to be a continuing relationship behind the public stance.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the -- the question that we were debating within the UN and I think many within the international community generally was how deep were the divisions between Belgrade and Pale, between Yugoslavia and between the Bosnian Serb Republic. I think very considerable tensions had been generated by the failure of the Bosnian Serb leadership to accept either the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in 1993 or the contact group plan in 1994. I am not sure that I would go as far as to say that there was a political rupture between Belgrade and Pale, if you like, and indeed the -- the meeting that is referred to here and other subsequent meetings indicates perhaps that both sides were eager that the break didn't go too far. I should also say that there were a lot of indications that while there were undoubtedly tensions on the political side, these were not evident on the military side, I believe, between the Yugoslav military and the -- the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 6. It's a document dated the 15th of October, 1994, and it's from Mr. Stoltenberg to the Secretary-General. I want to draw your attention to the second page of that document and it has an assessment of Mr. Milosevic's relationship with the Bosnian Serbs. Can I ask you just to comment on the last line, which says, "His game plan" -- referring to Mr. Milosevic -- "is that either the present Bosnian Serb leadership should accept the Contact Group map or they should be replaced." Could I ask you to comment on that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well -- and clearly Mr. Stoltenberg in his cable to the Secretary-General underlines the fact that Mr. Milosevic had accepted the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contact group plan, but this clearly had not been accepted by the Bosnian Serb leadership. He speculates that there might be a possibility that the Bosnian Serb leadership could change in this regard. And I suppose there was a precedent in this respect, namely with the leadership of the so-called RSK, the Krajina Serb Republic in Croatia, where there had been a change in leadership. There had been elections which had brought to power there in, if I recall, January 1994, Mr. Martic, who pursued a policy line which was far closer to that pursued by Belgrade and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read a paragraph, or a sentence from the next page in the document. And it is Mr. Stoltenberg's assessment of Mr. Milosevic. I want to ask you if you concur with his assessment. "President Milosevic for his part, gives the impression of a disciplined power-player, bent on predominance in the overall Serb leadership, who could well prevail, and who has clearly-thought-through ideas about the shape of future political options affecting the Croatian Serbs as well as the Bosnian Serbs." Do you concur with his assessment of Mr. Milosevic during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's a very accurate and perceptive assessment. In that regard, I recall some 18 hours of meetings in Belgrade during the Gorazde crisis, on the 22nd and 23rd of April, 1994, a meeting presided over by President Milosevic in which a very large number of the Bosnian Serb leadership was present; I guess at least 10 or 12. And I think certainly Mr. Milosevic gave the impression, as Mr. Stoltenberg underlines here, of a disciplined power-player, of presiding over people who were not as equal in terms of political leadership and of decisiveness and of an ability to factor in all the different questions that had to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this same time period, based upon the information that you had available to you at the time, what information did you have with respect to General Mladic's presence in the Belgrade area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Now, are you referring to April 1994, referring after the -- August 1994 and the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if you take both those periods separately, if they're --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think -- excuse me. General Mladic was frequently in the Belgrade area. He did, of course, have family there. The first time I met with him was at this meeting in Belgrade that I referred to on April 22/April 23, 1994. I recall vividly that that meeting -- one thing I recall is that I think he -- it was the only time I recall him in civilian clothes. He was wearing a black suit and black shirt because he was still in a period of mourning from the death of his daughter, who had committed suicide. My recollection is that she had, in fact, been a medical student at Belgrade University. But I think both before the imposition of sanctions in August 1994 and afterwards, the indications we have are that General Mladic was a frequent visitor to Belgrade, that no matter what the political tensions were that were self-evident in the relationship between Belgrade and Pale, these did not seem to affect unduly his comings and goings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to a document; it's Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 7. It is during this period after the imposition of sanctions. If I could ask you to refer to the third page of that document. And this document is dated the 6th of March, 1995 and deals with a meeting between General Smith and General Mladic held on the 5th of March, 1995. And my question to you is: Does this UN report reflect the presence of officials from Belgrade at this meeting between Smith and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's right. And I remember this incident very clearly. I recall Colonel Baxter, the MA to General Smith - General Rupert Smith, the British commander in Bosnia - calling me before the meeting to chat about it. One of the things that made it unusual was that the meeting, as the document I think makes clear, was inspired by General Mladic. Virtually all other meetings, to the best of our recollection, were at the behest of the UN. Now, in his report and also in subsequent observations that he made, Colonel Baxter pointed out that while they were at Jahorina, the ski resort near Pale where the meeting took place, they saw several officials from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to the next document, 470, tab 8. And if I could ask you to look at page 3 of that document. There are two portions I would seek to read to you and ask for your comment on. And the first one is -- and I'm reading from the third paragraph on that page: "A Joint Commission was also created to draw up the modalities of the proposed unification of the RS and the RSK." Were you aware during this time period of attempts being made to unify the Republika Srpska and Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I mean, these -- this meeting was public, and my recollection is that, you know, there were press releases and so on. I'm not sure how serious I thought that possibility was. And I -- my assessment is that this was clearly something which would have made the conflict wider and have drawn the Croatian and Bosnian wars, if you like, together into one. It would have crossed recognised international borders between the two UN-member states of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it was a ploy that was entertained from time to time by Dr. Karadzic. I think he didn't find a willing suitor in Mr. Martic in Knin. Mr. Martic, I think, would have been more heedful, perhaps, of advice from Mr. Milosevic in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to put another couple of sentences to you and then ask you a few specific questions. And I'm reading from the sentence immediately following the one I just read. "Reports from the session indicate a serious rift having developed between the military and the political leaderships in Pale, aggravated by the ongoing economic blockade and the struggle for limited financial and material resources. It would appear that Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb political establishment face the prospect of a further erosion of authority; a process tacitly encouraged by Milosevic. The meeting between Milosevic and Mladic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "The meeting between Milosevic and Mladic in Belgrade on the 21st of April, which was allegedly convened without Karadzic's knowledge, would support that contention." My question to you is: Can you describe, using this document and in the context that you were working in, the relationship between Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Karadzic, and General Mladic, the relationships between those three people.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I mean, that's very difficult because clearly those relationships were conducted for the most part a way from public glare. But there are certain things I think we know. One is that both Mr. Milosevic and General Mladic in a certain sense shared a common history, a common history with regard to service to what was initially the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They were both members of what was the ruling and fairly monolithic Communist Party, the League of Yugoslav Communists. They'd both been members of that party, I think, from -- basically from sort of university days. Whereas, that was not quite the background of Dr. Karadzic. He had never been a senior official in the -- the old Yugoslav government. He had, if you like, been thrown up by the tempest of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the beginning of the wars of the Yugoslav dissolution, in 1990/1991, General Mladic - I think he was still -- perhaps still a colonel there then - was in Croatia, in the Krajina area, and it was only subsequently in 1992 that he was moved to Bosnia and promoted to general and appointed head of the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, during this time period, with this assessment by Mr. Akashi was drafted in April 1995, was there a sense among the UN mission at that time that the relationships between the three men was in a state of flux?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think so, because there was -- there was enormous pressure. There was the fact that Mr. Milosevic had accepted the contact group plan; the Bosnian Serb leadership hadn't. The situation on the ground in Bosnia itself was quite fluid. Pressure was building up on the UN to take more conservative reactions with regard to the Bosnian Serbs. So there were pressures there. Also, the Republika Srpska depended, I think, to a very considerable degree on support, financial, material, and otherwise, from Serbia. The Republika Srpska is not a very well-endowed region. There was virtually no functioning economy during this period other than smuggling; smuggling incidently which made quite a number of the Bosnian Serb leaders, I think, quite wealthy individuals and which allegedly earned the scorn and dismay of General Mladic, which I think is partly what this paragraph refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now shift to another topic entirely. You a few moments ago referred to Mr. Martic. Could I ask you to summarise for us your view of the Republic of Serb Krajina, the situation in the Krajina during the time that you held your office.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I referred just now to the -- the fairly sort of bleak economic situation prevailing in the Republika Srpska. If that was the case in the Republika Srpska, the situation in the Krajina, the heart of the Serb republic in Croatia was even -- even more dire. There was some elements of subsistence economy, but people essentially got by from UN humanitarian deliveries and from support that was given by Belgrade. This was a very small area with really no prospect whatsoever of surviving as a cohesive, coherent, self-support supporting unity. I think in that respect that's why I believe the leadership there and particularly after the elections of January 1994 and Mr. Martic -- Mr. Martic's assumption of power, that leadership was more -- was more beholden to Belgrade, because it had no other options.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 9. And this is an assessment by Mr. Akashi dated the 1st of February, 1994, and it refers to Mr. Martic's winning of the election. I want to read a particular passage to you or a sentence and ask you: Do you concur with Mr. Akashi's assessment. And the passage reads: "The dramatic reversal of the election results can be attributed to the efforts of President Milosevic and his supporters in the RSK." Do you concur with Mr. Akashi's assessment of the results of that election?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. People in the RSK, I would say even more than Bosnian Serb Serbs, felt acutely vulnerable, felt that close ties with Belgrade were their only hope, and also the Belgrade media had quite a powerful influence in the -- in the Krajina republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi goes on to forecast that the relationship between the Krajina and Belgrade will become closer as a result of Martic's election. Do you concur with that assessment and did that in fact come to pass?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is an accurate assessment, and that I think is more or less what came to pass. I don't think that Martic himself was a very effective political leader, and I recall that in meetings Mr. Milosevic frequently referred really to Martic's weaknesses in some respects, his inability to control Babic, his political rival, and the -- the local assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit tab 10 of 470 -- I won't ask -- you've made some comments or there are some comments in that table, that's Prosecution tab 2. So in the interests of time, I will rely on your comments there. Could I ask you now to focus your attention on the enclave of Gorazde. Could I ask you to take us to the spring of 1994 and summarise for us the situation as it presented itself in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, the Court will recall that Gorazde is one of the safe areas in Bosnia, one of six areas declared a safe area by the Security Council in May of 1993. In the period beginning, I think, in the final week of March 1994, the -- the safe enclave of Gorazde came under attack from Bosnian Serb forces. By early April, i.e., the second week of that attack, it was very clear that that attack was a premeditated assault involving tanks and heavy artillery conducted with some considerable brutality, and no attempt whatsoever to -- to avoid civilian casualties. I would also like to put this assault in a wider context, which is this: The Court will recall that there was the crisis over Sarajevo in February 1994. That crisis had resulted in a NATO ultimatum, a NATO ultimatum which had led to the withdrawal of a lot of Serb heavy weaponry. Some of that heavy weaponry moved east to Gorazde. It was also the case, I think, that the Bosnian Serb leadership were somewhat embittered by the outcome of the Sarajevo crisis. And finally, I think that the other relevant factor here is that in March 1994, I think somewhat to the surprise of observers at the time, a peace agreement was negotiated between the Bosnian government, between the Bosnian Muslims, and Bosnian Croat forces. So overnight the situation in Bosnia was transformed, transformed in the sense that what -- whereas what had previously pertained was a war, if you like, involving three different armed factions, now two of those factions had made an accord, a peace agreement which basically held, and a peace agreement which moreover involved the intervention of the United States. The United States played a critical role in negotiating that agreement. Now, I think these developments unnerved the Bosnian Serb leadership. In the first place, they faced the prospect now of the Bosnian government perhaps being able to redeploy forces, and perhaps they were also concerned about a more looming involvement of the United States in the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period, what, if any, offensive actions by the Muslims in the enclave of Gorazde were ongoing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think my reaction to that would be with what and for what? The Bosnian government forces in Gorazde had very, very little in the way of heavy weaponry. I mean, generally speaking, throughout Bosnia at this time there was -- there was a great inequality between the weaponry at the disposal of the Bosnian Serb forces and weaponry at the disposal of the Bosnian government. This inequality and disproportionality was even more enhanced with regard to those forces within the enclaves because, by virtue of the fact that they were besieged, it was very difficult for them to obtain armaments from outside, so that the Bosnian Serb forces -- sorry, the Bosnian government forces within Gorazde would have had little weaponry heavier than machine-guns or mortars. In fact, I think there's -- there's a telling fact, I believe in the report of the Secretary-General to the Security Council, where he alludes to the collection of heavy weaponry. I think this is a report, by the way, the Court will find at Exhibit 20. He alludes to the collection of heavy weaponry and refers to quite a number of weapons found - this is after the hostilities in Gorazde - found on the Bosnian Serb side and only two or three weapons found on the Bosnian government side. With regard to attacks out, apart from isolated sniping incidents, the -- it would have been impossible for the Bosnian government forces to break out and to form some sort of corridor with Sarajevo. I mean, they would simply not have had the forces and weaponry at their disposal to carry out a military campaign along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, with respect to 470, tab 11, I'll rely on the comments in tab 2. Can I now draw your attention to tab 12, and in particular the second page of that exhibit. I'd ask you, if you would, to read and comment on the last sentence contained in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is the last sentence in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Beginning with "Andreev reported --"

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. This reads: "Andreev --" who was a senior UN civilian official in Sarajevo. "Andreev reported that Churkin had been in contact with both Milosevic and Karadzic and that both agreed that the shelling must stop. Their intervention appeared to have no immediate effect." This report is a report to New York from the UN force commander, dated the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to another document, dated the 13th of April, 1994. It's tab 4 of Prosecution Exhibit 470. So if I could ask you to look back to tab 4 for a moment. And if I could draw your attention to paragraph 2 of that document. I'll read a sentence from paragraph 2. And this is a -- a report from Mr. Akashi to Kofi Annan, who was then in charge of peacekeeping forces. And I read the sentence: "President Milosevic claimed that the Bosnian Serb attack on Gorazde was their response to the Muslim offensive, which the Serb side had been expecting particularly since the Washington Muslim-Croat accord." Can I ask you to comment on that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. You can see the reference to the Washington Muslim-Croat accord, and that was, I believe, part of the background to the attack on Gorazde, and I think it's interesting that Mr. Milosevic, in his meeting with Mr. Akashi on the 13th of April, drew attention to that. I have no problem with that at all. Where I would take issue is with the idea that there had been a Muslim offensive in Gorazde. I can see no evidence for that whatsoever. I mean, there were -- I recall Mr. Milosevic making similar remarks in a meeting that I was present at, the meetings on the 22nd and 23rd of April. But to my assessment, it defies any possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to the 16th of April and draw your attention to tab 13 of Prosecution Exhibit 470. This is a -- actually two documents. One is a press release and the other is an underlying report. Can I ask you: Do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I mean, the press release is something that I personally would have drawn up. And then the accompanying document that you alluded to is a chronology of the events on the 15th and 16th of April. And you can see in the course of this week that events in and around Gorazde are steadily deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that this chronology includes by-the-minute developments as they occurred in the Gorazde enclave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's right. In situations like this, there was very, very strict chronicling and registering of the unfolding of events. And these were events too which for the first time NATO had been involved in very, very limited close air support missions around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe NATO's involvement at that time.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, NATO had been responsible for the NATO -- sorry, for the no-fly zone imposed by the Security Council for some considerable time. It had also been subsequently authorised to provide close air support for UN forces if and when they came under attack from any party. That close air support was first authorised on the Sunday, the 11th of April. I recall the events because I was closely involved in them in a fairly dramatic day, when Serb tanks and artillery were firing directly into the Gorazde safe area and directly at civilian targets and also directly firing very closely at the building which was a former bank where UN officials were trying to take shelter. It was in these circumstances on the Sunday afternoon that a close air support mission was authorised, which, if my memory serves me correct, resulted in an attack on a Serb command and control position, which I think was -- was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your description of or your -- from where did you have the knowledge that there were civilian targets within Gorazde being actually targeted?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These came from reports. I think -- one factor which I'm not quite -- I can't recall now whether I mentioned this to the Court. Gorazde was the only enclave where there was not a UN military presence. There was in Zepa and in Srebrenica and of course in Sarajevo and in Tuzla. But there was not a UN military presence in Gorazde, other than a very small number of UNMOs, UN military observers. They would have been present together with one or two officials from the UN High Commission for Refugees and I think at least one official from the International Red Cross. In addition to these people, as the situation had deteriorated, General Rose, the British army commander in Bosnia, had managed to insert through the Serb lines a unit of British SAS troops. So the reports came initially from the UNMOs who had been present there throughout, and then subsequently these reports were complemented by the British unit which had entered Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 14. This is a -- an assessment by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. And if I could draw your attention to paragraph 3. Could I ask you to read that paragraph and then comment on its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "Given the attitudes so far shown by the Serbs, the credibility of today's agreement is low. In the meantime, there is no longer effective military defensive measures available to the BiH army for the town of Gorazde." I think that's a very bleak assessment made by Mr. Akashi, who on the whole would avoid making such assessments, unless, as I think he did at this juncture, believe that events were now moving in a very, very critical direction. He had tried, over a period of a week or more, to abate the concerted Serb assault on Gorazde without effect, and what Bosnian government resistance there was was clearly crumbling. Two days earlier, as we know, UN troops had come under direct attack. A British RAF aircraft had been shot down by the Serbs on the 15th of April. And I think behind Mr. Akashi's comments here were at this juncture a very pessimistic and bleak assessment. I could perhaps add that this cable is dated the 17th of April. I believe that this cable had a profound effect on the Secretary-General and Dr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who the following day, the 18th of April, wrote directly to the Secretary-General of NATO, who was then Mr. Manfred Worner of Germany, requesting that NATO as a matter of urgency look at the possibility of airstrikes on positions of the Bosnian Serbs in any and all of the safe areas in Bosnia where they were involved clearly in firing and attacks upon civilian populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention now to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 15. This is now a code cable from Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi. And if I could draw your attention to paragraph 7. Could I ask you to begin with the second sentence of that paragraph -- or perhaps just read the entire paragraph, and could I ask you to place that in context for us.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The paragraph reads as follow: "After the meeting, Ambassador Vorontsov informed Mr. Gharekhan" -- Mr. Gharekhan, by the way, was a senior UN official in New York -- "informed Mr. Gharekhan of Foreign Minister Kozyrev's efforts in Belgrade. According to this briefing, President Milosevic had 'instructed' General Mladic to stop attacking Gorazde, to restore UNPROFOR's freedom of movement and to permit UNPROFOR to deploy troops in Gorazde. These points were to be implemented on the 17th of April before your meeting with Dr. Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you for your comment on that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As you say, this cable came from Mr. Annan, then head of the peacekeeping department in New York, based on a briefing given by the Russian Ambassador Vorontsov, who clearly felt his minister, Foreign Minister Kozyrev, had been given undertakings by President Milosevic in Belgrade that the attack on Gorazde would cease. I must say there was no evidence that such instructions were given and my recollection is that the attack actually increased in its voracity in the coming days. My recollection, for example, is that on the 18th of April in the morning between 8.00 a.m. and 10.00 a.m., there were 42 incoming shells and one outgoing shell, which again gives an indication of the disproportionality here between Bosnian Serb forces and Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we can move ahead to the 22nd/23rd of April, to the culmination of the events you've been describing, can I ask you to tell us about meetings related to the Gorazde crisis that you attended during those days?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the mood of the UN, both in Sarajevo and in the headquarters in Zagreb, was one of deepening concern. It was a very somber mood. There were great misgivings and fears that Gorazde might collapse, that is, that all resistance to the Bosnian Serbs might collapse Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that a quite substantial civilian population would be at the mercy of forces which had -- hitherto had, I'm afraid, an appalling record of brutality in dealing with civilians under their control. I mentioned in my prior answer to you, Mr. Groome, that the Secretary-General had written on the 18th to NATO, imploring them to look at the possibilities of NATO air actions, i.e., of serious bombing attacks against Bosnian Serb positions if they were guilty of attacking safe areas. I think this is -- that this was a matter that caused consternation to Mr. Akashi. His fear was that NATO involvement would escalate the conflict further, perhaps bring Serbia directly into that conflict. I think with that in mind, he had in the course of the week had a number of contacts with President Milosevic. We at headquarters held our normal morning meeting on the Friday, April the 22nd. The mood was very tense, very somber. We knew that that day the NAC, the North Atlantic Council, the key decision-making body of NATO, was meeting in Brussels and that they would there address the Secretary-General's letter and were expected to issue their own ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs, which they, in fact, did in the course of the day. Mr. Akashi reflected on the situation. We had a very long discussion at the senior staff meeting. And then he -- he announced that it was his intention to fly to Belgrade, to fly to Belgrade, that he discussed this with President Milosevic, and that President Milosevic was able to bring together the Bosnian Serb leadership, that Akashi had hitherto had meetings with President Milosevic but -- and also with the Bosnian Serb leadership but never together, and he felt that this offered a hope, however dim, of rescuing a cease-fire from what otherwise looked like an imminent tragedy. I must say, I usually -- at that senior staff meeting Mr. Akashi's view was contested by several of us present. We were not sure what could be wrought out of a meeting in Belgrade. There had already been several cease-fires negotiated which had come to nothing. In fact, we had seen the assault on the safe area grow in intensity. We were also mindful of the Secretary-General's action, in directly engaging NATO, and felt that the unfolding of events had now reached a situation where it might have been better addressed by others outside of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to deal with some of the particular discussions that were held during the course of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi decided despite our deliberations in Zagreb that he would fly to -- to Belgrade. My recollection is then that a group of us went with him to Belgrade, by which time -- the time of arrival in Belgrade would have been late morning, approaching lunchtime. I recall that General de Lapresle, the fourth commander, who was accompanying Mr. Akashi, that at Belgrade airport had to -- had to assemble what was then a mini satellite dish for him to be in contact both Paris and Brussels because of the urgency of events now unfolding in Brussels, that the NAC itself was coming to a decision. He spoke from the airport tarmac with both Paris and Brussels. Following those conversations, we moved to President Milosevic's offices in the centre of Belgrade, where very soon we were in a Plenary Session, chaired by President Milosevic and containing a very large number of the Bosnian Serb leadership, I think at least 10 or 12 or them. Those discussions, as I say, must have started around midday, 1.00 p.m. They went through the entire evening until about 9.30, 10.00. We, that is, the UN, then retired for the evening to a hotel but reassembled the following morning at 9.00 a.m., by which the pressures were mounting very considerably. Mr. Akashi had had instructions from the Secretary-General in New York that he should -- he should not under any circumstances delay much longer returning from Belgrade to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the Secretary-General had in mind clearly the deliberations and discussions that had taken place simultaneously with the Belgrade meetings in Brussels on the 22nd of April, when the NAC had decided to issue an ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs, requiring their disengagement, an immediate cease-fire around Bosnia, withdrawal from a 3-kilometre zone, and withdrawal at a slightly later stage of all heavy weaponry from a 20-kilometre zone. Now, we had discussions along somewhat similar lines in Belgrade throughout that fairly long Friday, on the 22nd, and indeed for a couple of hours on the Saturday morning, Saturday, the 23rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you, during the course of that series of meetings, could I ask you to describe your observations regarding the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and the Bosnian Serb leadership that was present.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think I'm -- I think I'm minded of the observation that was made by Mr. Stoltenberg in one of the earlier documents that we reviewed in this session, and that is of -- of Mr. Milosevic being a powerful player in these events. My recollection is at the beginning of the meeting he acknowledged the seriousness of the situation and then put forward, as I recall it, a three-point agenda. Number 1 was the normalisation of the situation between the UN and the Bosnian Serbs; number 2, the situation in Gorazde; and number 3, the desirability of a cease-fire in -- in Bosnia as a whole. I think unusually for Mr. Akashi, who was not prone to intervene directly and to challenge Mr. Milosevic or others that he was dealing with straight away, he did challenge that straight away and felt that it was only one matter that we could address at these meetings, at least one matter in great substance, and that was the seriousness of the situation in Gorazde and the absolute imperative of obtaining a cease-fire or otherwise events would take a far more serious turn of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did the meetings conclude? What was resolved?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The meetings -- excuse me, the meeting concluded with a six-point peace plan that involved a cease-fire, involved Bosnian Serb withdrawal from a 3-kilometre zone, a disengagement of their heavy weaponry, a promise to allow the UN unhindered access to Gorazde - a promise, by the way, which was never implemented, never seriously implemented - a stipulation that a number of medevacs, medical evacuations by helicopter, could take place of seriously ill and injured people out of the enclave. Again, a promise which was only implemented in the initial days of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 16. Do you recognise these documents? And if so, tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This is tab 16 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise these documents. This is a press statement which I would have drawn up myself in Zagreb on Saturday, the 23rd of April, after we had returned to Zagreb from meetings in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the -- the other document in this exhibit, it's a report, a code cable from Mr. Akashi dated the 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct. This is a report of the discussions in Belgrade to headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do they accurately reflect what transpired during the course of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit tab 17. And if I can draw your attention to the first paragraph of that document. It's a document from de Lapresle to Mr. Annan dated 25th of April, 1994. The sentence I'm asking you to comment on is: "The situation in Gorazde has stabilised as the BSA forces have completed their withdrawal to the 3-kilometre line agreed upon between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Akashi in Belgrade. This phase of the operation is now complete." Can I ask your -- your comment on that particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Groome, which is the sentence you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is the paragraph 1 of tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Beginning with: "The situation in Gorazde..." It's also on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I see the sentence now. This was a report filed -- would have been filed on the Monday. And it was true at that snapshot in time when this cable is written on the Monday morning that Serb forces had withdrawn from that 3-kilometre exclusion zone. We'll find, however, that within days Bosnian Serb forces are back in that kilometre zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention now to tab 18 of Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: May I refer to the Court to one other point in that cable, which is para 4, which I think is an important point. It's the final sentence of that para, which I will read, if I may: "The BSA demolition of the water filtration plant may, however, have serious humanitarian consequences in the coming weeks." I draw the attention of the Court to that sentence for this reason: This was a clear and premeditated assault and demolition on a water plant. That act was not untypical of Bosnian Serb military behaviour. The consequences of the destruction of the plant will, I think, be obvious. And in fact, from that date, April 1994, for the next two and a half years, until late 1996, there was no proper water supply in Gorazde; water was obtained only from the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention now to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 18. It's a short letter from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Milosevic, dated the 10th of May, 1994. Could I ask you just to read a couple of sentences that comprise the letter and then place it into context for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "As you may know, the situation around Gorazde continues to be difficult. The implementation of the agreement --" I'm sorry. "The implementation of the agreement reached in Belgrade under your outstanding leadership has encountered some insuperable difficulties. I have taken the liberty of enclosing a letter I have sent today to Dr. Karadzic in the hope that you may be able to help reach a quick resolution of the matter which indeed does not brook any more delay." There is then an accompanying letter which Mr. Akashi sent to Dr. Karadzic and which is quite detailed about very, very clear Bosnian Serb violations of the agreement reached only two weeks ago in Belgrade: Presence of heavy weaponry within the zone, obstacles to UN convoys, one convoy alone being delayed at a roadblock for six days, medical evacuations not taking place, so on and so forth. I think Mr. Akashi was -- was deeply disappointed that this agreement, the agreement reached in Belgrade, had not had an enduring effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 19, we'll rely on the comments contained in tab 2, but is it correct that this is a response from Dr. Karadzic to the letter that is contained in tab 18?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct. And this response comes from a member of the staff of Dr. Karadzic, Jovan Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to draw your attention to is Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 20. If I could first draw your attention to paragraph 19 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it difficult to follow. What's the essence of his response, the response from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Dr. Williams, to address Judge Kwon's query about Dr. Karadzic's response. Perhaps if you could summarise his response for us.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I would summarise his response, Judge Kwon, as peremptory. Dr. -- Mr. Zametica, an adviser to Dr. Karadzic, acknowledges receipt of the letter from Mr. Akashi. He doesn't really address any of the concerns in Mr. Akashi's quite detailed letter other than to say that he does admit that they do have uniformed men - he doesn't call them soldiers, he calls them "uniformed men," which is an interesting distinction - within the 3-kilometre exclusion zone. He argues, in fact, that they've been demobilised and they don't have any other clothes to wear, they're no longer people at war. In short, I mean, this is not a substantive and serious response to the detailed letter submitted by Mr. Akashi to the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can take you back to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 20, paragraph 19. It's just two sentences. Could I ask you to read that and place that into context for us.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "On 14 May 1994, my Special Representative, spoke with President Milosevic, who had assisted in the convening of the Belgrade meeting on 22 and 23 April 1994. President Milosevic assured him that he would do his utmost to bring about the prompt conclusion as well as the full implementation of the arrangements described in the preceding paragraph." Namely, the preceding paragraph refers to ongoing concerns with regard to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I draw your attention to this report to the Secretary-General - it's tab 20 - to paragraph 4 of that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there something that bears comment by you on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think this paragraph above all underlines the seriousness of the -- the situation that prevailed around the time of the Gorazde crisis. The paragraph refers to the Secretary-General's letter of the 18th of April to Manfred Worner, Secretary-General of NATO, requesting him to obtain at the earliest possible date a decision to launch airstrikes against artillery tanks in and around the safe areas which are determined by the UN to be responsible for attacks against civilian targets. He then goes on to say that on the 22nd, namely the Friday, Dr. Worner had informed him that two decisions had been taken on the protection of the safe areas. With regard to Gorazde, there must be a pull-back within, I think, 48 hours, out of the 3-kilometre zone; and that secondly, there must be a cease-fire, that the UN must have unimpeded access, and then there must also be withdrawal of heavy weaponry, all this on pain of airstrikes by NATO. I think the seriousness of this paragraph is this: That it is probable that without the meeting of the 22nd and the 23rd in Belgrade that airstrikes would have taken place against the Bosnian Serbs. I do not think that they would have withdrawn to the satisfaction of NATO, that NATO frankly had placed, if you like, higher hurdles for them to achieve, had set a far more rigorous parameter for the conclusion of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Dr. Williams, I must warn you, as we warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, I want to take you back to the meetings of the 22nd and 23rd of April in Belgrade and just ask you a few detailed questions. During the course of that meeting, did Mr. Milosevic ever express his view regarding the genesis of the Gorazde problem?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that he did. And it essentially somewhat amplified, it was along the lines as reported by Mr. Akashi following his earlier meeting with Milosevic on -- on the 13th of April, namely that Mr. Milosevic saw the origins of the crisis around Gorazde as being a Muslim offensive out of the enclave. He also referred, I believe, a number of times to this being Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that meeting, a day and a half, did you form an opinion with respect to Mr. Milosevic's views of General Mladic and Mr. Milosevic's views of Mr. Karadzic? And if you could compare and contrast those views for us.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a difference, which of course stemmed from the fact that Dr. Karadzic exemplified the political leadership and Mr. Mladic the military leadership. The political leadership was always somewhat cumbersome, inasmuch as they were always present in meetings in considerable force. One wasn't dealing as one more usually is perhaps in these sort of meetings with two or three senior officials; it was 8 or 10. And they were also somewhat shambolic is perhaps a word that comes to mind, sometimes in their internal arguments, in their unwillingness to address the issues at hand, especially in this case in the discussions on the 22nd and 23rd of April, 1994, because the matter at hand was so serious. By contrast, General Mladic was far less deliberative where he would express a view in this or in other meetings where I was present. He was often quite decisive, quite forceful. My recollection is that these meetings in Belgrade he was somewhat withdrawn inasmuch as I -- I think this was not so long after his daughter's suicide, which I presume had clearly had an effect upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that meeting, were you present when Mr. Milosevic directed Mr. Karadzic to make a phone call with respect to a situation that had arisen in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Rogatica is a village I guess about equidistant between Sarajevo and Gorazde, where a UN convoy which the UN had been trying to send to Gorazde with humanitarian supplies and including additional peacekeepers had been held up for several days, and as is often the case not just held up by but subject to harassment by the Bosnian Serbs locally. I recall Mr. Milosevic expressing impatience with this and saying, I think quite explicitly, that it was in the best interests of everyone that this convoy got through to Gorazde as soon as possible, getting somewhat ill-tempered be Dr. Karadzic and then asking Dr. Karadzic to instruct his officials in Rogatica that these obstacles should be removed and should be removed as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic comply with that direction?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I move from Gorazde, I want to draw your attention to one final document, and this jumps ahead to the 1st of April, 1995, and it is Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 21, and it is a report from Mr. Craig Jenness. And I'd like to draw your attention to the second page of that document, and paragraphs 1, 2, 3, and 4. I'd ask you just to -- you've mentioned this briefly in your testimony already, but I'd ask you just to summarise those four paragraphs. And in particular, could I ask you to identify the different civilian targets that Mr. Jenness felt were in jeopardy because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As you say, this document is dated April 1995, i.e., exactly 12 months after the events which have been concerning us. He refers to shelling in a completely random pattern of the town of Gorazde. He says that he is advised by military colleagues that this is -- that there is not controlled targeting, no attempt to -- to hit military targets. He says that there is clear targeting of the town centre where the hospital is located, social welfare centre, the Red Cross office, the UNHCR office, the market, and numerous cafes. All these sites are well known to the Bosnian Serb army, which has direct line of sight -- I beg your pardon -- which had direct line of sight into town from the surrounding hills. He concludes by saying "There was no local provocative activity by the Bosnian army forces before the attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the very next page, the last sentence of the first full paragraph. Does Mr. Jenness relay in his report a comment evidencing the rationale of the attack on Gorazde and one that was relayed to him by a member of the local Serb authority?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he does. And the quotation is from a local Serb official: "You squeeze Serbia. Serbia squeezes us. We squeeze you."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn your attention to Sarajevo. Can I ask you to summarise for us in what context you became aware of events in Sarajevo during your tenure.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I would have first visited in Sarajevo in February of 1994. This would have been after the incident in the marketplace of February 5, where quite a considerable number of civilians were killed. I subsequently visited Sarajevo on, I would have thought, at least 10 or 12 occasions over the next 12 months, often accompanying Mr. Akashi, on other occasions travelling on my own to meet with officials working for me in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Chamber briefly what types of measures would you have to undertake or would be undertaken for you to ensure your security while being -- being present in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These would vary, and they'd vary according to the situation at the time. I should also say to the Court that there were many occasions when I couldn't travel to Sarajevo because the air bridge, the UN aircraft which flew on a regular basis from Zagreb to Sarajevo, was not working because the flights had been either threatened by Bosnian Serb forces or directly shot at by Bosnian Serb forces. If I might give the Court one illustration of that: In the crisis on Gorazde, for example, the force commander's plane, when arriving in Sarajevo on the 17th of April, was deliberately shot at by Bosnian Serb forces, an issue that the force commander raised with Dr. Karadzic, who did not deny that -- that accusation. So there were times when I couldn't get there, but even on those occasions when I did, one would always have to take some security measures, including, for example, wearing flak jackets, helmets, or travelling in protected vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you use the word "air bridge," are you referring not only to the ability of international -- members of the United Nations or the international community to enter and leave Sarajevo but also for humanitarian aid to be brought into Sarajevo via the airport?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Humanitarian aid, medicines, food, and so on was in large part delivered by air. There were periods when it was possible to run road convoys into Sarajevo, but that in many ways was even more exposed to Bosnian Serb harassment, especially in the sort of 16-month period of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Akashi ever appeal directly to Dr. Karadzic to keep the -- the air bridge open in conformity with UN Security Council resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Frequently, repeatedly, and at every meeting I attended with Mr. Akashi with the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the result of such requests?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would vary. It was normally met with hostility. "Why should we be doing this to help the Muslims?" was a usual refrain. Repeatedly the Bosnian Serbs said that they wanted to renegotiate the situation of the airport, that the airport was their airport, and that the UN was privileged to -- to fly there. Sometimes during meetings they would make direct threats to safety of aircraft. To give an example of that: In September of 1994, the Pope, for example, had expressed a wish, a desire to visit Sarajevo. Mr. Akashi had mentioned this to the Bosnian Serb leadership in a meeting, who said quite clearly that this would be an unwise move and that they could not guarantee His Holiness's safety in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
