utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 22. It is a rather large packet of documents which you've had a chance to review yesterday. Can I ask you just to summarise what is contained in that packet of documents.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think this series of documents underlines the precarious position of Sarajevo. The fact that this was a city under siege, if one means by -- if one accepts the meaning of the term "siege" as to be a military encirclement of an urban population, denying access from and to that city or population, this obviously varied in degrees. The documents here reveal that humanitarian convoys frequently came under fire. A British convoy on July the 27th, 1994, for example, was directly targeted by Serb gunners, involving the death of a British soldier. Civilians were -- faced extreme dangers, were often subject to sniping at various times, some shelling, but I have to say less shelling after February 1994 when an agreement had been reached to withdraw heavy shelling -- sorry, heavy Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weaponry from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In this particular exhibit -- does this particular exhibit reflect Dr. Karadzic's views regarding sanctions and his response with respect to the civilian population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I mean, he at almost every meeting I recall saw the siege as a weapon of war against the civilian population, openly referred to the interdiction of humanitarian deliveries, to the disruption of utilities, whether it be water, gas, or electricity, to the denial of medical facilities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to a particular part of this document. And it is, for the Court's benefit, ending in ERN 2892. It is an excerpt of a speech by Dr. Karadzic. It will be displayed on the television screen in front of you. And that may be perhaps the easiest way to view it. Are you familiar with this --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm very familiar with this document. This was a speech given by Dr. Karadzic in Pale to the Bosnian Serb National Assembly, where quite clearly he makes threats against the civilian population of Sarajevo, quite explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And those threats to be realised by what means?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: By, inter alia, the disruption of -- of supplies to the city and by imposing sanctions on its inhabitants. I think here is a particularly telling phrase, or rather, a chilling phrase at the end, one which I actually heard him use a number of times in meetings. If I may repeat it to the Court: "I think now that we have full right to introduce such sanctions against Muslims, that even a bird will not fly through to them until the world forces Yugoslavia to lift economic sanctions against the Bosnian Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Williams, if I can for a moment go back to some of your prior -- or experience, your experience prior to testifying today. Did you for a time -- were you a member of the International Institute of Strategic Studies?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was a Senior Fellow IISS in London in 1995 to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based upon your scholarship and experience, can you help place the context of the siege of Sarajevo in the broader historical context of other sieges that have existed in this century?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The concept of waging siege obviously goes back to early times in the history of -- of warfare. It was something that -- it was a tactic, a strategy that was indulged in during the Second World War, particularly on the eastern front by both the Germans and the Russians. However, I think it's striking that in the period since the end of the Second World War, since 1945, despite conflicts and wars that have taken place in almost every continent of the globe, siege warfare is actually somewhat exceptional, somewhat exceptional. In that respect, I think the conduct of the Bosnian Serb forces with regard to the various safe areas in Bosnia and also earlier the conduct of the Yugoslav forces with regard to Vukovar is quite exceptional. Exceptional I think in two senses: I mean, one, it not being typical of most of the warfare that has transpired since 1945; and secondly, exceptional in the brutality and rigour with which those sieges have been implemented, with very, very clear targeting of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you now place the siege of Sarajevo in the context of the other events transpiring in Bosnia at that time, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In the time that I was in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there had been some easing of the situation in Sarajevo following the crisis of February 1994. The shelling of the city, which had been a regular feature since 1992, ceased as Serb heavy weaponry withdrew from a NATO-imposed exclusion zone. For a very brief period after February, two months or so, there was greater humanitarian access by road and by air into Sarajevo. From April onwards, I think coincidental with the Gorazde crisis, the position in Sarajevo began to change again for the worse, a deterioration which became more marked by the end of 1994 and which continued into 1995 and which resulted in deprivation of most utilities for the civilian population and the frequent interdiction of humanitarian supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you, in brief terms, describe what was the situation facing Bosnian Serbs at the time, and was humanitarian assistance to them ever interrupted in a systematic way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was humanitarian assistance to the Bosnian Serbs, but the question is, I suppose, interrupted by whom? The humanitarian agencies have their obligations, obligations which are written into international humanitarian law that the Court will be aware, and into the mandates of these organisations. And that, barring logistical problems, severe winters and the rest, that humanitarian aid did get through to the Republika Srpska, which is not to say that the economic conditions of many people in the Republika Srpska was not difficult. Their conditions were very difficult. But that difficulty stemmed in essence from the fact that here was an entity which had no real means of economic subsistence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 23. It's a letter from Mr. Akashi to Dr. Karadzic. I want to draw your attention to the second paragraph of that letter. It reads: "I am sure that you would not intend to cause suffering to innocent civilians and I would urge you to refrain from taking any such actions whose effects would be devastating on the lives of innocent people, especially in Sarajevo and the Eastern enclaves, and would dramatically escalate tension." This warning to Dr. Karadzic, was this one of a number of warnings to place Dr. Karadzic on notice about the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And this particular warning had been prompted by the speech that we referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. You know, Mr. Groome, it's really very difficult if one is given a bundle of documents like this with unpaginated and undifferentiated documents, and I'm referring to tab 22. And one of the issues which arises is the date of the speech. Now, no reference has been made to that, but I see looking at it that one can, if one looks at the fax number, see that if the fax is dated the 20 -- or rather, the 2nd of September, if you look at the bottom of the page. You also irritatingly have to use upside down reading. If you do all that, you will find the 2nd of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies for that particular exhibit. Perhaps I could ask the witness if he has an independent recollection of when that speech was given.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that that speech would have been given, I believe, on the evening of the 1st of September, 1994, that the translation of the speech was then faxed to me by the Reuters correspondent in Sarajevo, and that then Mr. Akashi subsequently wrote to Dr. Karadzic on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you could return your attention to tab 23. That reference to Eastern enclaves that Dr. Akashi makes when he refers or puts Dr. Karadzic on notice, to what specific locations is he referring?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi is there referring to the three Eastern safe areas, namely Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa. Now, if I have talked earlier about the difficult situation of Sarajevo, those difficulties are many times multiplied by the situation that prevailed on the ground in those three enclaves, which were entirely dependent upon access by road. There was no -- there were no airports or airfields with which to facilitate air supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The -- the things that occurred in Sarajevo that characterised it in your mind as a siege, did you see similar evidence in other places in Bosnia or similar tactics?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. For example, Gorazde. We referred earlier to Mr. Jenness, the officer that I'd placed there. I relied to a considerable degree on his very regular reporting. Gorazde was subject to quite frequent shelling, despite the Belgrade agreement of April 22/April 23, 1994. As I pointed out to the Court earlier, during that attack the water filtration plant had been deliberately destroyed by Bosnian Serb forces. There was no power in the -- in the enclave, except the power provided -- excuse me, the power provided by fuel generators which provided enough power for two hours a day. And it will be obvious to the Court the difficulties that this would introduce for the hospital and for children, elderly, and the sick in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to 470, tab 24. I will rely primarily on the comments contained in tab 2. This is a -- a code cable from Mr. Eagleton to Mr. Annan and Mr. Akashi, dated the 19th of September, 1994, once again discussing the cutting off of gas and electric and how it affected the civilian population of Sarajevo. My question to you is: During this time period, was there any significant military activity in the Sarajevo area that would justify such measures?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I could agree that any military activity would justify such measures. In fact, my understanding of -- of the Geneva Conventions would be that disruption of essential utilities, such as gas, water, and electricity, would be something that should be avoided by all armed parties. But certainly there was nothing in this particular period which prompted, as Mr. Eagleton points out in his cable, the fact that the Bosnian Serbs had closed the valves on the gas supply to the city, gas providing the heating for the vast majority of the city's inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention now to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 25. If I can draw your attention in particular to paragraph 3. It's the bottom of the second page of that exhibit, and it is a quote of Dr. Karadzic. Could I ask you to, please, read that quote and then continue on the next sentence and comment on that portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "In his words" -- that is, Karadzic -- "'If the international community treats us like a beast, then we will have to behave like a beast.' He specifically mentioned, in this regard, the use of utilities as a means of war. As the afternoon progressed, he mellowed somewhat, indicating he might consider restoring electricity, water, and gas to Sarajevo if this were done in the context of repairs to utilities in Bosnia as a whole."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Would Mr. Milosevic have been made aware of Dr. Karadzic's views with respect to issues like utilities and their use against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he would have. I think these are matters that Mr. Akashi would have brought to his attention. Indeed, as we saw earlier with -- with Karadzic's remarks at the Bosnian Serb National Assembly these were matters of public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic ever express what his goal for Sarajevo was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He spoke of a -- a division of the city. He spoke approvingly of the division of Berlin or of the division of Beirut. Two examples: He was -- he was, I have to say, fond of referring to -- he said that in the future there were to be two cities, completely separate, and rigorously demarcated in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to draw your attention to the shelling and sniping in Sarajevo. There will be other witnesses that will be called to testify about their observations. My question to you is: Did you yourself personally -- were you personally present during one occasion when a young woman was the victim of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. And I should say that sniping was a regular occurrence. There were periods when it was more intense than others, and there was attempts -- there were attempts by the UN to secure so-called anti-sniping agreements, one of which was in August 1994. Having said that, such incidents, as I said, were quite regular and I did on one occasion see a girl who was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe in -- can you please describe the incident that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I was walking back to what was then the UN headquarters, the so-called residency, from the Holiday Inn Hotel, where I'd been holding a meeting with journalists and was walking back and heard some shots run out and saw a couple of hundred yards away that a young girl had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When would this have been?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My recollection is that this would have been in September/October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were -- was there any international military personnel there at the scene?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Very fortunately, there were. This was an area that was known infamously as sniper alley, and because of that was fairly regularly patrolled by French forces. And as luck would have it on that day, there was near at hand a French vehicle which took the injured girl to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At that time, did members of the French force express their view regarding from which direction the sniper had fired?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They said the fire had come from buildings occupied by Bosnian Serbs on the other side of the line, buildings which were frequently used for sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to shelling, did you ever complain to General Mladic regarding shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the margins of one meeting in Pale, and said that I'd found this was utterly reprehensible conduct that conflicted with the laws of war and also with the specific agreements which pertained to Sarajevo after the February crisis. He replied by saying, "We will always send two shells for every shell fired by the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he referring to shells fired by the Muslims from Sarajevo or from another part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think from Sarajevo in that instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention briefly to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 26. Is this a press briefing that involves your own drafting, your own work?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time during your work in Sarajevo that you became aware of an increase in Serb air defences around the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Serbs drew some lessons from the crisis around Gorazde in April 1994. They had clearly seen the threat of NATO airstrikes. And by the autumn of 1994, our military colleagues within the UN were reporting increased Serb air defensive measures not only around Sarajevo but also in North-Western Bosnia as well, these measures including greater deployment of radars, frequent locking-on to aircraft by Serb radar, and also increasing number of surface-to-air missiles being deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the conclusion of where this new or additional air defence equipment came from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The conclusion was that it must have in less considerable quantities had somehow been in storage, which I think is questionable. The conclusion was that it must have come from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was this the assessment of Mr. Akashi and also the military personnel who were present in --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention to Bijeljina. Could I ask you to summarise the situation in Bijeljina, Bosnia, during your tenure in your office.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Bijeljina was one of those towns which in some ways it had escaped some of the worst excesses of the onset of the war in 1992; in this sense, that some minorities had remained there, as they had in Banja Luka. I think in the case of Bijeljina, for example, my recollection is that there were approximately 7.000 Muslims living there, together with a small number of Romanies. Beginning in mid-February -- sorry, beginning in mid-July 1994, the Red Cross alerted us to the fact that very large numbers of Muslims were being forced out of their homes in Bijeljina and forced to cross into Bosnian government lines. In fact, over the next month, 2.500 Muslims were forced out of their homes in Bijeljina, and then from September to November a further two and a half thousand. So most of the minorities there were forced out in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this same period, were Muslim families required to take in Bosnian Serb refugees to live in their homes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were. And this seemed to be a practice particularly prevalent in Banja Luka, which was the other area where there was still a concentration of minority peoples living. I was always struck by the extremely dark picture we had of reports of life in Banja Luka for Muslims and Croats, a life which I think they endured with dignity but which was one of terrible deprivation of access to basic medical supplies, even of rights within death, inasmuch as Muslims who died were not allowed to be buried in Muslim burial places. But the injunction to take in Serb refugees in your home was a very frequent one, and in fact subsequently some Muslims said to me that in some ways there was even some benefit to it inasmuch as at least you could hang on to a corner of your home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the situation in Banja Luka, could I draw your attention to tab 42 of Prosecution 470, and in particular the third page of that exhibit, number 6. You may not have it. I'll ask the usher to bring it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is a fax from Mr. Stoltenberg to the Secretary-General dated 27th of June, 1994. Under Roman numeral VI, Mr. Stoltenberg writes: "During our meeting with President Milosevic, I raised with him the situation in the Banja Luka area and told him that what was taking place there was unacceptable. In reply, he said he would prefer not to comment." Were you aware of this interchange between Mr. Stoltenberg and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was aware of this, this cable and the report of the meeting, and indeed I think that Mr. Stoltenberg's intervention with Mr. Milosevic has been prompted by continuing and in many cases harrowing reports of the situation prevailing in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 27. I apologise in advance to the Chamber. This is another series of several documents. The only one that I will be referring to in any detail is the last page, and that's ERN ending in 4223. Take a look at that exhibit. Is it fair to say that this is a series of press releases by both ICRC, the UN, and other organisations regarding the situation in Bijeljina during 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it's a situation that was raised many times with the Bosnian Serb leadership, I regret to say with no effect, other than that Dr. Karadzic feigned at one point to have removed a local police chief, who he said had been responsible for harassing Serbs -- I'm sorry, harassing Muslims in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention now to the last page. It's a letter from Mr. Akashi to Dr. Karadzic dated the 20th of September, 1994. Are you familiar with this letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I think I assisted in the drafting of this letter. I think it was an unusually strong letter, Mr. Akashi to write to Dr. Karadzic. He speaks of his utter dismay at the continuing expulsions of Muslim civilians from Bijeljina. He writes, for example, of 700 arriving on one single day, on the 17th of September. And he also draws the attention of Dr. Karadzic, which I think was the first time he did so, of the possibility that such deplorable acts, that those responsible for continuing such criminal acts would be subject to investigation and prosecution by the International Tribunal on War Crimes in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At some point, did you discuss with Dr. Karadzic the destruction of mosques in the area controlled by Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did. And in fact, it would be -- it would have been fairly near this point in time. I went to Pale on my own and had meetings with, first of all, his advisor, Jovan Zametica, and then with Dr. Karadzic himself. I wanted to raise access to the eastern areas. But I also want to raise with him the deliberate destruction of places of worship and places of historical importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did he say in response to or as the reason for the destruction of mosques in the --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He -- I was taken aback that he said that he didn't deny that mosques had been deliberately destroyed. He said they had been destroyed because these were symbols of Turkish imperialism and that the wrath of the people in this matter should not be thwarted. He said quite explicitly that it would be a good thing if all aspects of that heritage were erased.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can briefly turn your attention to Tuzla and the presence of an airstrip in Tuzla. Can you begin by describing what significance from a humanitarian point of view that airstrip held.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Tuzla is actually -- it's quite a large airstrip. Tuzla is also one of the safe areas declared by the Security Council in May of 1993. Despite the presence of this quite large airstrip near the -- the city, the -- the UN had been unable to use the airstrip because the Bosnian Serbs said, We do not want supplies going into this airport to Muslims. Mr. Akashi on March the 1st, 1994, as I recall it, decided to -- to present a fait accompli, as it were, and together with quite a large group of journalists and senior officials we flew on a UN aircraft carrying humanitarian supplies from Zagreb to Tuzla. The reaction of the Bosnian Serbs was one of fury. They said this hadn't been cleared with them, that any further flights would be targeted by their forces, and for good measure, as it were, thereafter they fairly regularly targeted and shelled the airstrip. I should say there were no further UN flights for many years after that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now, if I can turn your attention to the Bihac pocket. Can you summarise your observations regarding events that took place in the Bihac pocket in and around 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Bihac is quite a large pocket, situated in the north-west of Bosnia where, more than in other pockets, I think there was a substantial presence of Bosnian government forces; and indeed I think beginning on October the 23rd, 1994 there was a Bosnian government attack out of the Bihac pocket. That attack was -- initially had some success, but within a fairly short period of time, certainly by November, Bosnian Serb forces were able to take an offensive and to -- to press back on the safe area of Bosnia -- sorry, the safe area of Bihac. I think their ability to undertake that attack is interesting because, of course, at this time they were supposed to be under sanctions from the Yugoslav authorities. Mounting an offensive necessitates the use of considerable quantities of fuel and obviously of -- of ammunition, and certainly the Bosnian Serb forces showed no sign of being short of either. Indeed, they were able to redeploy forces at some quite considerable distance from Eastern Bosnia to North-Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, I want to draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 28. It's a code cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, and it relays a meeting with Mr. Tudjman. If I could draw your attention to paragraph 4, the last sentence of paragraph 4 contains an assessment by Mr. Tudjman which reads: "But whatever the configuration of the power game in Knin, all players have ultimately to answer to Belgrade." Did that concur with your assessment of the political situation in Knin during that period?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it did. I think I mentioned earlier to the Court the position of the Croatian Serbs in the so-called Krajina Republic was far more precarious and vulnerable than that of the Bosnian Serbs in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention to a completely different subject. During the course of your work, was there considerable concern about the possibility that the Yugoslav army was still taking an active part in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. events in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe in summary fashion before I ask you to comment on particular documents about this phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, everybody, I think, was aware of the fact that both the forces of the so-called Krajina republic and the forces of the Bosnian Serb republic had their origins in the old Yugoslav army, namely the JNA. And there did not seem to be any indication that the parentage of, if you like, the parentage of those two forces, the Croatian Serb forces and the Bosnian Serb forces, had been relinquished. In fact, on the contrary: What one saw was a fairly regular rotation of officers between the JA and Bosnian Serb forces and Croatian Serb forces and the ability of both the Croatian Serbs and the Bosnian Serbs to undertake some operations for which they did not on the surface of it have sufficient logistical and technical capability. I mean, one aspect of this, for example, would be helicopter flights. Another aspect of this would be the strengthening of the air defence system in Bosnia in the course of 1994. I mean, you cannot simply build an air defence system out of nothing. You can't do that overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 30. And do you recognise what that document is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a code cable to Mr. Akashi from New York, from Mr. Annan, referring to reports in the New York Times of the -- regarding the presence of Yugoslav army officers and allegedly vehicles in Eastern Bosnia in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it also accompanied by a letter by a member of the permanent mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to read the first paragraph of the letter, summarising the media reports up until that time regarding the possible involvement of VJ or Yugoslav army troops in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That reads as follows: "We regret having to express our deepest concern about reports over the past several days by our Government as well as international media, informing us of renewed and intensive deployment of Yugoslav Army troops and armoured vehicles coming mainly from three directions: from Serbia through Bijeljina, Zvornik and Visegrad. This is only the latest evidence of blatant Serbian and Montenegrin aggression against the internationally recognised, sovereign and independent Republic of Bosnia..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would this information or these claims have been brought to the attention of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I -- I have no categorical recall of that, but I would have expected them to have been brought to his attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this code cable is dated the 31st of January, 1994. Could I draw your attention to tab 31, which is a document dated the 2nd of February, 1994. First, can I ask you to tell us what the Yugoslav Daily Survey is or was, and then to please comment on the first paragraph, the statement of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Daily Survey was a press survey of the sort that most missions to the UN produce on a fairly regular basis, to -- to keep people informed of their various countries. Now, the issue in the -- that you refer to here on February the 1st cites Mr. Krajisnik, who was president of the Assembly of the Serb Republic, as saying there was not a single soldier from the FRY on the territory of the Bosnian Serbs and the RS was not receiving any arms from the FRY. He goes on to mention a radio report, most categorically denying the information in US circles that the VJ - i.e., the Army of Yugoslavia - are crossing into the RS to fight on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified earlier about the introduction of sanctions. Was there ever any discussion with Mr. Milosevic with respect to the monitoring of the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My recollection is there was. As I recall it, Mr. Milosevic accepted the contact group plan in the summer of 1994 regarding Bosnia. The Bosnian Serbs, however, did not accept that plan. And Mr. Milosevic, I think on the 4th of August, announced sanctions against the Bosnian Serbs, against the Republika Srpska. There was subsequent discussion, I think, that Mr. Akashi and Mr. de Mello had, as well as Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg with Mr. Milosevic on the desirability of some monitoring of that sanctions regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Monitoring by whom?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That -- that was initially left open. The obvious body to do it, I mean, given its deployment in substantial numbers throughout the former Yugoslavia, was the UN, was the United Nations protection force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And indeed, after Mr. -- the sanctions were announced on August the 4th, some scoping assessments were undertaken by the UN with regard to the possibility of a monitoring force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was Mr. Milosevic's position with respect to having international observers in Serbia to monitor that border?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think he was hesitant and reluctant to see such a force deployed. He pointed out, I think, to the political difficulties that this would cause within Serbia itself and argued that, of course - which is true - that Serbia was a sovereign territory and I think initially reluctant to see such a force deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the monitoring force that was eventually deployed along the border.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What was eventually deployed, which was I think was on September the 17th, which is about six weeks after the announcement of sanctions, was a force which came under the aegis of ICFY, the International Conference of Former Yugoslavia, which was a negotiating mechanism, not a field force. It was a negotiating mechanism at this stage headed by Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg. That force, as I recall it, was about 135 strong, to try and monitor a body -- I'm sorry, to try and monitor a border of 300 miles' length.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your view, was it an effective monitoring system, able to seal the border?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have to say no. In the initial planning done by the UN, two options were put forward. One would have been for a deployment of a military force on the Serbian side of the border, and under this plan the deployment of 4.000 soldiers was envisaged. As an alternative, there was the option of deploying a mixed civil-military force, UN military observers plus civilians, which would have been 700 strong, and which it was felt could have been adequate for monitoring the border. I think the ICFY force was too small in number, that its ethnic base was essentially Scandinavian, and that its officials did not have access to the information and intelligence that NATO forces would have had access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I seek your brief comment on Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 32. Does this outgoing code cable to Mr. Annan, dated the 31st of January, 1994, discuss some of the problems involved in monitoring the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It does. And it talks -- I mean, monitoring borders, frankly, is difficult in any part of the world. They had some particular difficulties in the former Yugoslavia dictated by the terrain and the topography, the mountains, and so on. And the then-force commander, General Cot told New York that it was really impossible to closely monitor any of the borders of -- between Croatia and Bosnia or between Bosnia and Serbia and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 34. It's a -- it's a note to the file regarding a meeting between Mr. de Mello and Mr. Milosevic on the 9th of August, 1994. If I can ask you to take a look at paragraph number 7. It has a representation by Mr. Milosevic about the border. And I'd ask you to read the sentence beginning "The border is completely sealed." If you could read that and continue on to the end of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "The border is completely sealed; only food, clothes, and medicine will be permitted passage. He emphasised that the exceptions to the blockade were not grouped under a vague category of 'humanitarian goods' to avoid ambiguity. Rather, they were strictly defined as 'food, clothing, and medicine.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the end of that paragraph, he goes on to say, "This is not Brazil...our borders can be effectively made hermetic." Did the international community rely to some degree on Mr. Milosevic's assurance that he had sealed the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think to a very considerable degree. By the way, I think the reference to Brazil was because Mr. de Mello is Brazilian, and Brazil, of course, is a vast country compared with Serbia in size. Nevertheless, I mean, I think experience has shown in very, very many contexts that sealing borders is easier said than done. And one was struck by the fact that Republika Srpska seemed to get by despite the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 35. Does this document corroborate some of your observations regarding the border closure?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Groome. Tab 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can now draw your attention to tab 36 of Prosecution Exhibit 470. And if I can draw your attention to the second paragraph under Roman numeral I. This document is a report from Mr. Stoltenberg to Mr. Goulding, Mr. Annan, and Mr. Akashi, dated the 6th of September, 1994. That first sentence -- the first sentence of that second paragraph reads: "President Milosevic and President Bulatovic both assured us that the closure of the border was being implemented strictly and that this would continue." Did Mr. Milosevic regularly assure the international community that the blockade was effective and was being observed by Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a few minutes ago in your testimony about helicopter flights. Can I ask you to speak to that issue in a little greater detail with respect to helicopter flights that were observed from Serbia into Republika Srpska or Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And the Court will see some documentation at tabs 37 and 38 and also at 39. This was a frequent problem, and it was one that seemed to increase with the implementation of sanctions. I was aware of helicopter flights originating from or going towards Serbia and beginning in September 1994. Indeed, I gave an off-the-record briefing to the press on that, which I believe appeared in the New York Times on the 21st of September. Flying -- and these were helicopter flights quite often in some considerable numbers, 5, 10, and 15 helicopters flying at night. This is no easy operation. Helicopter flying in such numbers at night is a very difficult undertaking and one that needs considerable coordination of radars, ground radars, and the helicopters themselves in the air. We know from their own records that the Bosnian Serbs I think only had about 20 helicopters at this time. So the question arises: How are they able to put in the air 15 helicopters in one single place at one particular evening? I think that that defies imagination, that they would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there documentation made and an investigation conducted into these helicopter flights?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was documentation. It's before the Court. There was an investigation. There were incidences, which are described in the documents, where UN military observers who were present at airfields in Serbia were denied access on more than one occasion, denied access to radars which they should have been able to access.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Williams, I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, this is a packet of several documents. The reports that Dr. Williams has referred to, the key documents of this report, the entire reports, have been supplied for completeness, but the Prosecution seeks to rely primarily on the maps that are contained in these reports showing Bosnia-Herzegovina with lines indicating radar tracks of observed aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that they be played on the screen in front of you, Dr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are these -- the documents, are these -- do these lines on these maps indicate detected aircraft flying from Serbia to Bosnia-Herzegovina or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, particularly that one on the map of the 23rd of February, for example, you see considerable movements towards Serbia out of Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the ultimate finding of the investigation into -- I'm sorry, before I ask you that. Approximately how many in total detections were made of aircraft violating the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Gosh, I mean, a very, very considerable number. I can't put an approximate figure on it. But one thing I'd like to point out to the Court, for example, was that, you know, in Srebrenica, as the Court will be aware, there were Dutch forces on the ground which were adequately equipped to undertake aerial observation. In the enclave of Zepa, for example, the only UN presence was a Ukrainian force, which I fear was -- was perhaps less well equipped to undertake aerial observations. So in fact the -- the maps that you have before you and so on may to a considerable degree underestimate the amount of aerial traffic taking place at this period of time in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What were the official published findings of the investigation into these transgressions of the border?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that the -- the published findings of the report were that essentially there was a case to be answered here and that it had not been adequately dealt with by the -- the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did that also confirm -- or conform with the privately-held views of the members of the UN mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I draw your attention up to the Croatian border with Eastern Slavonia, and are you familiar with another violation of the border in which there was an investigation into a Russian general.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe that incident to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That incident, which I believe took place in late March/early April 1995, involved military equipment coming into Eastern Slavonia from Serbia proper. And in Eastern Slavonia there were Russian and Belgian units present as part of the UN force. And on certain dates in question the Russian officer commanding, General Perelyakin, requested the Belgian forces not to interfere or hinder the transport of military equipment coming from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 40 -- I'm sorry, 470, tab 40.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe what that document is.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This document is a code cable from New York, from Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi, in which he says that the American mission there has officially approached us on instructions that they believe that an incident -- the move had taken place - i.e., military equipment had entered from Serbia - that most of this equipment was already registered with the UN, although he does qualify that, except for six tank destroyers and two Howitzers, and this equipment was being transferred from one part of the Serb Krajina republic to another part of the Serb Krajina republic via Serbia. The cable goes on to say that "The US considers this a gross violation of Security Council resolutions and wishes to have a full explanation," and in particular it raises the question of the complicity of the Russian battalion in the movement of this weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there other concerns with respect to violations of sanctions regarding this Russian battalion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have to say that there were quite considerable, and those concerns led, very soon after this, to a request being made to the Russian federation to withdraw immediately General Perelyakin and from Croatia, which was undertaken with -- with some deliberation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to tab 41 of Prosecution Exhibit 470. Is this another report from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan with respect to this incident which you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when did you finish or complete your service in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I finished that service on April the 17th, 1995 and then returned to London, where I took up a position as a Senior Fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies and where a large part of my tasks and duties included the assessment and analysis of the developing situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you left a few months prior to the tragic events of July 1995 in Srebrenica. During your 15 months in the former Yugoslavia, were there tangible objective signs that if the enclave of Srebrenica were to fall a humanitarian crisis on a grand scale would have followed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was. Personally, throughout my service in the former Yugoslavia, I felt very considerable concern as to what would happen if one of the attacks prosecuted by the Bosnian Serbs went through to its final conclusion, namely that an enclave, a safe area, would fall into their hands. I think their record from the onset of this war in 1992, and certainly in the 16-month period I was employed there, showed not only an inability to distinguish between civil and military targets in war but, on the contrary, a deliberate targeting of civilians during warfare and also continuing when areas they had taken were occupied. One only had to look at the situation of minorities in the Republika Srpska, which I think is -- has virtually no comparable incident or effect outside of the Second World War in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Setting aside the precise number of people killed in Srebrenica, could anyone with intimate knowledge of the events of the former Yugoslavia in 1994/1995 have been reasonably surprised that military-age men were killed after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I think if I go back to the Gorazde crisis, there was a period when everyone from the UN military observers in Gorazde itself, up to and including Mr. Akashi, were very, very fearful of the consequences of what would happen when Bosnian Serb forces entered the city of Gorazde. I think our conclusions were that there would inevitably be civilian casualties, that these would be serious civilian casualties that would involve gross violations of human rights, and that frankly the only question in our mind would -- would have been the degree and extent of those casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 470, tab 29, the third page of that exhibit, paragraph 9. This exhibit is a report from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan dated the 25th of February, 1995, which contains Mr. Milosevic's view on the situation as it existed in Bosnia. Could I ask you to read the first sentence of paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "President Milosevic concurred that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina would deteriorate and blamed it on the international community's focus on 'details and not the situation as a whole.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your view, as of February 1995, did Mr. Milosevic equally appreciate the gravity of the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think he did. We were stumbling all the time from one crisis to another, from Sarajevo in February 1994 to the Gorazde crisis in April 1994, to Bihac in October and November, and it was obvious, given the continuing deterioration on the ground in Bosnia and around the Eastern enclaves, that one could premise a further crisis and deterioration in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could reiterate the meaning of the accused's comment, which says, "... the international community's focus on 'details and not on the situation as a whole,'" as you understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Judge Kwon, my -- I think my understanding of that would be that Mr. Milosevic would have been arguing that too often the international community perhaps had been focussed on the particular crisis, the series of crises I just alluded to in Sarajevo, in Gorazde, in Bihac, and that one had to see these in the round and that peace would only come with -- with an overall agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what would be the situation as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the situation as a whole would have been a cease-fire throughout Bosnia and some form of political settlement. I think that as the war had gone on, and certainly by 1994, when the war was -- had been running two years, the Bosnian Serbs and I believe Mr. Milosevic wanted to see a settlement and a settlement on the best of terms, obviously. They were particularly mindful of the fact, as I mentioned somewhat earlier, that peace now -- a peace accord had been implemented between the Muslims and Croats, and in that respect this had obviously been a boost for the Bosnian government. It had also indicated a growing involvement of the United States. So I think there was a feeling perhaps that time was not on their side and that the prosecution of the war needed to be brought to an end somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes. And then we'll have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Williams, in your response to the last question and commenting my position, you quoted a passage and said that I said that the international community was engaged in details and did not look at the situation as a whole. Which is true. I think that we share each other's opinion on that score; we agree. Now, are you aware of my position ever since the beginning of the war in the former Yugoslavia, in view of its character - the character of the conflict, I mean - and that it couldn't be put right by seeing to details, that details could not solve the war and that the war had to be stopped?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I am familiar with your views. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is that what actually happened? The war was indeed stopped when there was a comprehensive agreement in Dayton, after which there was no more war, nor any incidents either.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is a fair conclusion. I would, however, say this: The United Nations, and particularly Mr. Akashi during the period when he was there as head of the UN mission in 1994 and 1995, had to be concerned with the detail, and you will know as well as anyone that the detail and the whole cannot be separated, but especially in the circumstances prevailing in 1994/1995, because I am afraid that time and time again in Sarajevo and in Gorazde, in Bihac, and ultimately in -- in Srebrenica, Bosnian Serb forces pressed home assaults, ending with -- with we know what happened in Srebrenica. So the detail could not be separated. And indeed, as in the discussions which took place with you on April the 23rd and April the 22nd, 1994, it was -- the detail had to be addressed first, because the people in the safe area of Gorazde were under direct attack. I wouldn't argue with you when you conclude that the war obviously was brought to a conclusion by Dayton. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I think -- if I may continue just a little, I think that agreement, frankly, could have come much sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I think too, and I'm sure you'll agree that we're not -- it's not a question of either/or here, either the details or the whole. Of course, both the details and the whole is what we're looking at, and the advantage goes to the comprehensive and overall -- rather, end of the war; whereas, the details could take second place. Isn't that right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would disagree with you there, I'm afraid. And I think often the details are the -- the essence of the matter. It was impossible in the circumstances, for example, around the Gorazde crisis of April 1994, to move forward to a general cessation of hostilities because we couldn't even deal with the emergency surrounding Gorazde. That meeting on April the 22nd and the 23rd, although it brought to a halt the Bosnian Serb attack, there was continuing shelling, continuing presence within exclusion zones, continuing denial of access of -- of UN convoys, and so on and so forth. If that agreement had been, frankly, fully implemented, then I think it would have made possible progress towards a general cessation of hostilities, which Mr. Akashi earnestly wanted, and of course that was the reason behind the meeting in Geneva, in June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is something that I advocated the whole time. I assume you're not going to deny that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not going to take issue with that. But what I have to say is, you know, the nature of the conflict that unfolded in Bosnia in that period, although it was a war, was exemplified above all by concerted Bosnian Serb assaults on areas which had already been declared safe areas by the Security Council of the United Nations, and it was difficult in those circumstances, I think, to move to a general political settlement. You refer to Dayton and the success of Dayton, and I think, frankly, that is one of the most remarkable things about Bosnia today, the fact that Dayton has held. In my experience, there are not many peace agreements in the modern world that actually hold in a consistent way like that over what is now seven, eight years. But one of the reasons why that has held is that the international community demonstrated quite forcefully, because it had to, that it would not tolerate any longer Bosnian Serb attacks on civilian populations and in particular on areas declared safe areas by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But to conclude, to round off this question -- and Mr. Williams, could you please give me as short as possible answers to my questions, because my time is limited. Do you share the opinion of a compatriot of yours and the co-presiding officer of the conference, Lord Owen, after Dayton, that the war could have ended two years before with the same results, had there been the true support on the part of the international community. And above all, he spoke about the US administration and President Clinton. I'm sure you'll remember that. Do you share that opinion of his?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do and I do not. I do in this respect, that I think the war could have been brought decisively to a close earlier only if the international community had taken decisive action against the Bosnian Serbs at an earlier date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand your approach, Mr. Williams. It stems -- it would appear, it seems, that it was only the Bosnian Serbs that went to war and that there were no other parties to the conflict and war according to what you say in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that is an assertion which you make. The witness should have the opportunity of dealing with it. It's suggested that you're one-sided to that extent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the opportunity to speak to that. I have to deny that, Mr. Milosevic. And I certainly have to deny the validity of that remark with regard to most of my testimony, which revolves around the 16-month period in which I served with the UN in the former Yugoslavia. For most of that period, the predominant military activity was that prosecuted by Bosnian Serb forces against Bosnian government forces, which is not to deny at all there wasn't military activity by the other side and indeed not to deny that there wasn't military activity initiated by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And it is precisely this period that you just mentioned, as I understand it your post implied an insight into all the documents that were sent to the special representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Akashi, both civilian ones and military ones, and that you had access to all the reports and documents that were collected by the UN rapporteurs, monitors, and by the national military contingents which made up the UN forces. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the course of this relevant time, material period, you were a representative of UNPROFOR for the public in the former Yugoslavia; right? And you coordinated the information programme. You were the spokesman, in fact, were you not, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is a correct description of my -- of my work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, from that, can we deduce that you were in fact, speaking in general terms, the best informed person who was representative of the UN in the former Yugoslavia during the time that you were present there and to which you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I'd hesitate -- excuse me, I'd hesitate to use that formulation of the best informed. I think that Mr. Akashi was -- was better informed in many ways and a number of other senior officials. But I would say that I was well informed amongst a sort of tight group of senior officials that served with Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm very happy to hear that, and I hope that we're going to have an opportunity to hear Mr. Akashi's testimony personally. Tell me this now, please, Mr. Williams: Can we at least then assume, along with the reservations that you made, that you coordinated the information programme of UNPROFOR, that you compiled statements for the world public coming from the region? Were you in fact the individual who selected these materials and had under your control the flow of information, the type of information put out, which communique would be put to the media and published and so on? Just give me a brief answer to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, together with officials who worked for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true and correct that objectively speaking you weren't able to look at all the daily, weekly, and other reports and compile them in the form of communiques for the press and public but that you did so on the basis of a selection you made?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question there, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that there was a lot of information coming in, I assume that you couldn't take all of them into account and you had to select some of the pieces of information and reports that came in to you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Clearly I tried to work to the best of my abilities and also to ensure that those who worked for me and with me had at their disposal as many sources of information as possible in order to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you dealt with activities at the university, you did work of that kind, and of course looked into a well-defined subject matter - you had clearly-cut positions and relationship to the matter you delved in - now, the selection of material from the period of time we're talking about, on the basis of that selection were you able to separate your own views and positions and the information that you selected from the field, on the ground, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I was. Rigour and objectivity is something that I've always felt to be important, frankly, in all the professional duties that I've had to equip myself of during my career, whether as a servant of the United Nations or currently of -- of the British government or as an academic in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Williams. Now, in view of the fact that a large portion of your statement refers to the events in Sarajevo, give me a precise answer to this question: How many times did you personally go to Sarajevo in the course of those years, 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would have said in the course of that year between 10, 14, or 15 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many times were you in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was never in Gorazde. I asked on several occasions to visit Gorazde. In fact, earlier in my testimony you may recall I referred to a meeting I had with Dr. Karadzic in late September 1994, and part of the -- the reason for that meeting was to request his assistance that I be able to visit Gorazde. I was never able to obtain that permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, may I take it then, and conclude, that what you're saying, to the greatest possible measure, is based on the reports from observers on the ground; is that right? That was what was it was based on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: With reference to Gorazde, yes. I mean, that would be wholly based on reports on the ground. I mean, subsequently after the Dayton Agreement, when I was working in different capacities, I visited Gorazde, but never during this period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But then we imply and mean that the observers on the ground, as they were able to see and witness things firsthand, they were undoubtedly more competent than you to assess the situation or to testify to the events that happened at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously with the immediacy of -- of events. Sometimes - and the Court will be well familiar with this - however, that an individual on the ground clearly has a snapshot of events unfolding, sometimes it's possible further -- from further afield to put together many different aspects of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please, Mr. Williams: While you were performing your functions, did you have any doubt into the objectivity of some of the observers on the ground at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Are you referring now in particular to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Gorazde and the other people who reported back to you, because if you did have, I'd like to see who you had your suspicions about or doubted in any way as to the authenticity of the reports and verisimilitude.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, for example, you referred to Gorazde. What strikes me, when I look back at my period of service with the UN, was the consistency of reporting from Gorazde. Initially when the Bosnian Serb attack began in late March 1994, most of that reporting came from UNMOs, UN military observers, or from UNHCR. In order to supplement and to verify that reporting, a highly-skilled SAS team was sent to Gorazde, which reported remarkably similar findings. And then at a later stage, I sent my own personal representative there, as it were, Mr. Craig Jenness, dealing with the later period of time, the end of 1994, early 1995, and his reporting was very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we're not only discussing Gorazde. As you had in mind the overall picture, did you doubt any of your observers on the ground? And if so, whom did you doubt?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I mean, some reporting is more detailed, more incisive than -- than other reporting. And I think one had to put that -- put those reports alongside others. Also, some areas were easier to obtain reports on. Now, for example, the UN - and for that matter the international press corps - were present in quite substantial numbers in Bosnian government territory. But with regard to the Republika Srpska, as I alluded to in my earlier testimony, it was very difficult to get reports because of the systematic denial of access by the authorities, both to the UN and to the press corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I'm going to ask you once again to try and be as brief as possible in your responses to my questions because my time is limited. But let's be precise, as we don't seem to be able to clarify this point. Do you consider that somebody, for example, who was an SMO, as you said, or senior military observer, for example, so this senior military observer who was on the ground, who was equally competent as you yourself were on the ground and in testifying to what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, as I'm afraid is in every other field of professional endeavour. I mean, some military observers were better than others. I mean, just as some journalists are better than others in what they report. But in Gorazde, even in the most difficult period, for example -- I mean, there were teams present. So if you like, the strengths and weaknesses of one observer would have been supplemented by those of another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the basic duty of the person who was an SMO, a senior military observer, on the ground was to govern and command -- control and command of military sectors in Sarajevo, for example. If you can just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'd give you a yes answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we're on the subject of Sarajevo, do you know what Lima and Papa teams are? And give me a yes or no answer, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try and refresh your memory on that score, well intentionally, of course. I don't want to set a trap of any kind by asking this question. Is it true that the military observers in Sarajevo were divided into two teams, in fact, the Papa team, in charge of the Muslim side, and to see how they opened fire, determining the casualties on the Muslim side, holding links with the brigades and police stations, hospitals in their area of responsibility and so on, to monitor Muslim activities generally up at the frontline, to investigate the situations if this was warranted by the senior military observer - I'm sure you'll remember what they were now - and on the other hand, we had the military observers in the Lima team. They had the same tasks and assignments for the Serb side. Does that refresh your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many military observers were included into the composition of the Papa team and how many in the Lima team? So the Papa team and the Lima team.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't, off the top of my head. No, I'm afraid I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According my information, there were six members in one team and seven members in the other; six in the Muslim team and seven in the Serb team. But we could say that the number was equal.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know who Francis Thomas Roy is?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not an individual I'm familiar with, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that he was a high military observer for Sarajevo, an SMO, in the course of 1994 around Sarajevo, and that under his command he had both these teams, in fact, both the Lima team and the Papa team?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, during the time you performed your functions, did you yourself personally, or anybody else, have any comments to make with respect to his objectivity on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. But for the clarification of the Court, the UNMOs were only part of the military presence in Sarajevo. Of course, there's quite substantial headquarters presence, led by General Rose, plus there were the French battalions that were present in Sarajevo. So their own work supplemented that of the UNMOs you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but my question is: Do you know that Francis Thomas Roy, just like you yourself, made a statement here in Court, on the 18th of April, 1998, in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. May, in order to identify the statement, so Francis Thomas Roy, the number is 00908234 up to 00988238 [as interpreted]. Those are the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Williams: Do you remember the date of the 20th of December, 1993 when it comes to Sarajevo, for any particular reason? Does it ring a bell in some connection?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid it doesn't ring any immediate bell for me. I was not present; I was still in Cambodia at that stage, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. I'm going to quote something now. Are you familiar with it? Regardless of where you were, all the international media in their reports said that in the shelling of Sarajevo on that particular day, there were hundreds of people who were killed and wounded. I'm sure you'll remember that report. And it was a very memorable day, when all the world media said that there were several hundreds of people who had been killed and wounded on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I have to say to you, even though I was the other side of the world, and you know, I -- I'm an inveterate listener to BBC World Service, I don't recall that report, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, there's not much point asking the witness about it if he was in Cambodia at the time. You can ask a witness who knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to say to you that in Mr. Francis Thomas Roy's statement, which I referred to just a minute ago, I noticed that at that time you didn't have your headphones on, Mr. May, and I referred to a statement. He made that statement here just like Mr. Williams is testifying now. He said that the Bosnian side claimed that there were hundreds of killed and wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No point. You cannot ask the witness to comment on what some other witness has said in a statement. You can call that witness yourself or you can -- you can cross-examine if he's called by the Prosecution. But there's no point trying to cross-examine the witness further about this. You can ask him about the period that he was here, of course, if he was in Sarajevo. Of course you can ask him about that. There's no point asking him about events outside that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in view of Mr. Williams's competence, I'm asking you -- I'm asking him, rather, about his opinion about a media report that refers to hundreds of persons killed and wounded and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What date -- what date are you talking about? What date is this? If you're referring to December 1993, you've been told that it's irrelevant and you can't ask the witness about it. So you should move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm talking about the statement in which it says that there was a total of 17 persons killed. And I'm asking Mr. Williams to tell me what he thinks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what Mr. Williams, frankly, with respect to him, thinks about it at all. If you are talking about December 1993, you've been told not to. If you want to ask about another date, we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May. I did not assume that Mr. Williams did not think at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know, from the point of view of the actual establishments, who the warring parties were at the Sarajevo theatre of war? Rather, let me be even more precise in terms of this question. Let me not put any riddles to you. Do you know that on the Muslim side it was the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the name of the commander is Karavelic, as a matter of fact. On the other side was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you claim that most attacks, in all fairness in your opinion - you're presenting your own opinion - were offensive actions of the Army of Republika Srpska rather than defensive actions, and you claim that this is what the leadership in Pale invariably stated that. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since in your statement you talk about the Serb side only and their participation in the conflict, do you know that in the report made in 1998, Francis Thomas Roy's report, it says, "It seemed that the Serbs around Sarajevo were pursuing a position holding activity. I did not see them launch a single attack."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What can he say about that? What can the witness say? All he can say is the reports which he received, not whatever Mr. Roy said. Who is Mr. Roy, Mr. Groome? Can you help us? Who is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do not know, Your Honour. I'm having that ERN searched.
