utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned, when I quoted him, that this is a statement given on the 15th of April, 1998 and that Francis Thomas Roy was head of the Monitoring Missions in Sarajevo and that this is on pages from 00908234 up to the end of his statement, given, I presume, to Mr. Groome or one of the people working for him, because I got it under Rule 68. It was disclosed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I asked Mr. Williams, since it says here: "It seemed that the Serbs around Sarajevo were pursuing a policy of holding positions only. I did not see the Serbs launch a single attack." Now, does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've told you you're not going to put this. It's a waste of time, and you're not going on wasting the time of the Court like this. You can call Mr. Roy yourself, if you want. You can ask the witness what he saw and what was reported to him. You can ask him if he agrees, for instance, with the characterisation that it was a holding operation. Mr. Williams, can you help us with that? What is suggested was that this was merely a holding operation -- just a minute. You've put it, we will let the witness deal with it. This was simply a holding operation by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it depends upon the time on which you're speaking about, of course, in this three-year war. During the period I was there, initially there were - in January and February 1994 - there were quite serious attacks from the Bosnian Serb side, which of course led to the NATO ultimatum. After that point, the attacks diminished in their seriousness. I should also like to put on record that I do not deny that there were attacks by Bosnian government forces from time to time during the period in which I held my position in the UN, attacks by Bosnian government forces out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wish to draw your attention to the following,

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That Mr. Roy was a military observer from mid-October 1993 until mid-July 1994. So it also includes half a year of the time that you are testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but I should inform the Court that I've never met Mr. Roy. I'm not aware, I'm afraid, of his testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Williams, may I interrupt you. Nor should you be. In fact, it would be quite wrong for you to be. And it's fairly pointless, Mr. Milosevic, asking this witness about whether Mr. Roy is right or wrong. You can put things, of course, to him, such as it was a holding operation, but simply reading out his statement is simply not proper. Yes, your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you precisely instructed me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to ask the question of this witness, that is, whether he agrees with the assessment contained in the passage that I quoted to him, nothing more and nothing less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Bosnian forces made an effort to take the road to Pale, or rather, the Serb connection between Pale and Lukavica, very well equipped, as a matter of fact? The infantry was used, equipment was used against the Serb forces, and so on. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. And there was an attack in 1994, I think to try and seize part of the road towards Pale. I think, you know, in these circumstances it is helpful for the Court perhaps to -- to look at the weaponry at the disposal of the contending factions. And I think this is well documented by objective institutes, including the International Institute of Strategic Studies, and it's very clear from that information that with regards to tank, heavy artillery, helicopters, aircraft and so on, the equipment at the disposal of the Bosnian Serb forces was far greater in quantity and quality than that at the disposal of the Bosnian government forces. I would say that this is simply an objective assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Williams. But do you agree with the following assessment, also of Mr. Thomas Roy? He says in his statement - I'm quoting him now - but then you're just going to give me an answer as to whether you agree with this, whether this fits into what you know. "The Bosnians were prone to use heavy weaponry and they were shooting in order to provoke fire, for example, shooting from the hospital compound or placing a mortar in a coal-transporting train and then moving it behind the PTT building where the UN had its headquarters, and then firing," and so on and so forth. "Once when I stopped on the Serbia side on the Lukavica-Pale road, I noticed that the Bosnians --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What Mr. Roy noticed is neither here nor there, but you can put the generality of the matter. Mr. Williams, I think you've got the general point there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do. Obviously, I can't refer to the specific -- the specificities of Mr. Roy's testimony, but I did hear on occasion that the Bosnians had sited weaponry near a hospital in Sarajevo. I would acknowledge that I had heard that report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Williams, did you receive reports to the effect that they were seen armed or that they were shooting at close range from the hospital at Serb positions or from right behind the PTT building where the UN headquarters was in Sarajevo, and then they would withdraw afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't recall a specific allegation with regard to the position behind the PTT building that you allude to. There was firing from the city on a number of occasions towards areas held by the Bosnian Serbs. I would not deny that for a moment. And it is the nature, the ugly nature, perhaps, of urban fighting that weapons are frequently placed near civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since your very own military observer, an UNPROFOR military observer, says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, no. This is all comment by you. The witness can only say what he saw or heard. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness received reports. He was the main coordinator of the military observers in Sarajevo, and I'm just asking him whether he shares his assessments, and his assessments are quite different from the assessments made by Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you're making comments, which is improper at the moment. You can make them in due course. Now, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just offer one clarification. Military officials did not come under my command. They came -- they were responsible to a military chain of command which went up to, in the first instance, General Rose, the commander in Bosnia, and then to General de Lapresle. Now, I saw their reports, but it's not true to say that the UNMOs reported to me, and indeed they couldn't, being military officers and the fact that I was a civilian official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But did you take into account these reports of theirs when making your own assessments or did you not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did take them into account. You've raised the assessment of Mr. Roy that Bosnian Serb forces were conducting what you call a holding position, for example. I would contest that. The concept of a holding position conveys passivity, but in fact what was being pursued was an active policy of siege of Sarajevo. And in that respect, that the siege was exemplified by the repeated interference with utilities to the city and the repeated denial of access to the UN itself to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But a short while ago you said that Mr. Roy headed the military observers. As regards these war operations, do you believe that he is -- that he would be more competent, or rather, would a military or civilian expert be more competent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed something. Did you say that Mr. Roy headed the military observers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't, Judge May. I took Mr. Milosevic's word on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way we can get misled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I also make one further clarification? Because I think Mr. Milosevic is trying to make a distinction between military and civilian observers. Now, there were -- there were more than one set of military observers in Sarajevo. There were the official UNMOs, the UN military observers, but there were also the reports sent directly by the sector commander, who was a French general always, and by General Rose's staff at BH command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, overnight perhaps you could tell us, Mr. Groome, who this gentleman is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a copy of the statement in B/C/S. I'm working on getting it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, just for the transcript, since it is being contested here whether I properly quoted the position held by Mr. Roy in relation to his -- on page 2 of the B/C/S version of the statement, the last paragraph reads as follows, quite precisely: "On the day of the 15th of October, 1993, I became senior military observer for Sarajevo (SMO) - senior military observer - and I held this position until the 14th of July, 1994. My predecessor, the SMO for Sarajevo, was Lieutenant Colonel Kukula [phoen], from Finland, who remained in that position for four months, and I was succeeded by Major P. G. Sko [phoen], as an original."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've now got the position. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I asked you, Mr. Williams. How is it possible that the reports that you wrote are so substantially different from the reports of the UNPROFOR SMO on the basis of whose report you wrote your reports? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is -- it is possible in this way, Mr. Milosevic: My reports would have been based on a wide range of assessments, civil and military, a plurality of reports, not just from the UN military observers but from the Sector Sarajevo command, from BH command, from UN civil affairs officers, from the reports of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and where it was relevant, sometimes from reports from the international press based in Sarajevo. So the reports of the UNMOs were simply one stream of reports that I would receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that source, as far as military operations are concerned, to be more competent than journalists or the UNHCR or other sources? I imagine that they gave objective assessments too.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think everybody tried to the best of their ability to provide accurate assessments. Obviously, military observers are generally better qualified to comment on military aspects than they are, say, on humanitarian aspects, and the opposite would also be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted us to state here. And you mentioned a while ago that you were aware, from various reports, of attacks against Serb positions between Pale and Lukavica. You did know about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how and in which way the Muslim forces of the BH army, during the siege of Sarajevo that you have been talking about, they were being armed by high-quality equipment, French-made, for instance? Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you know the name of David Fraser?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid that's an individual I'm not -- not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me try to jog your memory. This is the military assistant to the French general who was commanding the sector in Sarajevo, French General Soubirou. And there was Captain Dedier [phoen] and three French bodyguards who were also on the French general's staff. So this was assistant commander of the Sarajevo sector. Let me just add one more thing. He held this position from the 17th of April, 1994 until the 26th of May, 1995. So this fully coincides with your stay there and what you have been testifying about, that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have to take your word for that. General Soubirou I knew and met several times, and I recall a Captain Dedier and his staff, but I have to repeat, I never met an officer by the name of David Fraser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have his statement here, also given to Mr. Groome's side, Mr. Groome being the person who examined you. The number is 00908284. This is something that was also disclosed to me according to Rule 68. So the time does coincide, doesn't it, with your time spent there? So it is from 1994 to 1995. And this is what his statement says. His statement was made in 1997; is that right? The dates do coincide with your own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go over this. We're wasting time. Now, I'm not going to let you put the whole statement again. You know what the rules are. What is there that you want to put which the witness can answer, as opposed to give an opinion or comment on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am first identifying the person involved, Mr. May, and then I put my question. So here it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What David Fraser says in his statement, is it true when he says, "When I arrived in Sarajevo --" and he did arrive on the 17th of April, 1994 -- "the 9th naval division of the French army was there, the bodyguards were from that division, they were succeeded by the 11th Airborne Division of the French army, which was the former division of General Gobillard. General Gobillard was the successor of General Soubirou, and it was the Light Armoured Division that came afterwards. That one consisted of legionnaires." Is this correct, what Mr. Fraser says?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's correct in its elements, as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me: How come the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had sophisticated French weaponry, state-of-the-art French weaponry, under the conditions of the blockade that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know about the weaponry, if it existed. So no point asking him about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If he doesn't know -- I mean, rather, I did not hear the witness say that he didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I thought I had alluded earlier to your question. I think you put to me whether I knew they had what you called sophisticated French equipment. The answer was no. I mean, it might help if you were able to be more specific. I mean, what does this mean, "French equipment"? What sort of weaponry are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just this, just this that I mentioned, which they got from the French, no doubt. I identified the units that were there, and I read them out from this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste further time on this. The witness has said he doesn't know about it. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the letter of protest that General Morillon sent to Alija Izetbegovic? It was entitled "Violation of the Geneva Convention." Since I have this letter of protest here, it is addressed to President Alija Izetbegovic -- [In English] Subject: Breaking of Geneva Convention. "You will, I'm sure, be aware that the firing of weapons from the hospital is against the Geneva Convention." [Interpretation] Then he goes on to say, and I'll leave out the details. He says: [In English] "82-million mortar had been set up on the western side of the Kosevo Hospital within the hospital grounds. This mortar and its crew then proceeded to fire nine rounds using the hospital as a screen. The direct consequence of this disreputable and cowardly act was that shortly afterward the hospital came under fire from anti-aircraft gunfire, artillery fire, and mortar fire." [Interpretation] And I'll leave out some parts again. [In English] "I'm also becoming increasingly concerned at the recent increase in indication of a lack of discipline -- a recent increase -- [Interpretation] recently increased [In English] -- "is an indication of a lack of discipline among your forces. I must urge you -- I must urge you to take immediate preventative actions. I regret also to have to inform you I have been asked to pass the details of this particular incident to the International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva." [Interpretation] So are you familiar with incidents of this kind, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- first of all, can you give us a date? What's the date of the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January 1993, written by General Morillon to Alija Izetbegovic. It is a letter that I have. And it's not the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, since it's a letter, although it's outside the time of the -- the witness, nonetheless it's a document. Let the witness see it, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, clearly it is a letter from General Morillon, as Mr. Milosevic said, dated 19th of January, which is a full 12 months before I assumed my position in Yugoslavia, and it does refer, as Mr. Milosevic says, to a very, very specific incident on 1430 hours, Monday, the 11th of January, 1993. That specific incident is impossible for me to speak to, I'm afraid. However, I am aware of reports, as I indicated in an earlier answer to one of Mr. Milosevic's questions, that on occasion there were reports of mortars being situated near the Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Since that's a document, we'll exhibit it. The Prosecution can have a look. If we could give it the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Defence Exhibit 147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let the Prosecution see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, does it appear to you that this letter in particular - and there are others - actually confirms the statements of Mr. Thomas Roy, a senior military observer, that I quoted from earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a clear matter for us. It's a pure comment whether it does or not, whether we hear from Mr. Roy or not. It's not for the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, is the UN headquarters -- or rather, the UNPROFOR headquarters, was it based in the post office building? Please say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, I think the answer is no there. The Sector Sarajevo headquarters were based in the PTT building, but the headquarters of BH command were based in what was called the -- the residency building, which is further up town. The answer is the headquarters for the Sector Sarajevo was based in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Sector Sarajevo headquarters were based in the PTT building. That is not in dispute, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, it's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following assertion: It says, "Bosnians were prone to use heavy weapons to disturb people and they opened fire in order to provoke fire, as they did from the hospital compound, for instance," et cetera. "They used a mortar in a railway truck and put it beside a PTT building where the UN was headquartered. They would fire and then move back." Are you familiar with this practice that they resorted to? And you have quoted once again from this senior military observer, a very particular concrete example of them bringing a mortar within the PTT compound, opening fire on Serb positions from it, and then removing it again, and that is what he testifies about on the page I have quoted. Do you consider that to be correct or not, or do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I -- I'm not in a position to pass an opinion one way or the other on that. I mean, I have never heard of a specific report, allegation, or statement with regard to the use of mobile mortars near the PTT compound in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I didn't claim this on the basis of any Serb sources but on the basis of a source provided by your senior monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't want, Mr. Milosevic, a running commentary on your cross-examination. What we want are the questions. Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Williams: How many reports about the attacks of the VRS against that particular command, from the immediate vicinity of which, as your monitor claims, fire was opened against their positions, were published without indicating that fire had been opened on VRS positions from that same spot previously? Or rather, does it mean anything that this building of the UN command was used as a screen behind which they would open fire on positions held by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I find it difficult to follow your question there. I mean, I do find it sort of outrageous to suggest that the UN building was used as a screen with -- you seem to be implying that with the -- with the -- the connivance of the UN. I'm sure that is not the case. Throughout the period that I served with the UN, great effort was made when firing incidents took place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. It was a confused and rambling question which was difficult to understand the point of. I think it may be, though, we've exhausted the topic, Dr. Williams. I mean, was there ever any suggestion to you that that building was being used for the purposes of -- of firing by the Muslim side, or anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the very best of my knowledge, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, to make things quite clear, I'm not claiming at all that there was any connivance between the Muslim side and the UN, with respect to the use of that building as a screen or shelter. On the contrary. On the contrary. Because if there had been connivance, then a military observer of the UN would not put this in his statement as a violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about what he said. We've -- we've been through this. Now, unless you've got some other topic of cross-examination, it may be you'll have to bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a sufficient number of topics. I hope you will give me sufficient time too, Mr. May. I understand that we're closing for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go on until five to, another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, if we don't take into consideration these facts which I am quoting exclusively using as my source reports of your own military observers, does that distort the image of the Serbs and their -- what they are called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I've told you more than once: This constant commentary and comments is irrelevant. What you say about your cross-examination is irrelevant. The fact that you say you're quoting monitors is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following statement, Mr. Williams, and I'll quote your military observer. I'm just asking you whether you agree with it or not. "The greatest advantage of the Bosnian Serbs was their great supremacy in tanks and artillery, but it wasn't of great advantage in fighting in built-up areas. Their use of artillery and tanks to shell Sarajevo in an attempt to influence the will of the Bosnian government actually had very little effect. The shelling to provoke terror and to discourage infantry attacks by the Bosnian side actually played into the hands of the Bosniaks (the Muslims) because the international media were accommodated in the Holiday Inn Hotel in Sarajevo and they tended to report on the war on the basis of the situation in town." That is contained in the report of this observer of yours. Did you receive a report to this effect from any observer from the territory of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I have no recollection of that specific report. I can comment a little on the content within that quotation. I notice that the observer clearly acknowledges the great discrepancy in weaponry between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Bosnian Serb forces and the Bosnian government forces. He talks about tanks and artillery on one side and infantry attacks on -- on the other. He also says, which I think has some truth to it, that awful though these attacks were upon the civilian population of Sarajevo, it is not the case that the morale of the population was broken, if that indeed was the objective of those attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I'm not raising the issue of the balance between the two sides. Let us leave that aside for the moment. I assume that you know that officially the government of Serbia, through the media and in public, condemned the shelling of Sarajevo. I assume that you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm aware that statements were made from time to time, not as forcefully --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what I wish to ask you here is: Is it clear that this was not a one-sided attack by the Serbs but a conflict between two parties on the frontline around Sarajevo? Is that at issue? Is that in dispute for you as a UN spokesman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is clear that a war was being -- was -- that a war was taking place and that Sarajevo was one of the focal points of that war. I think the most accurate description of the campaign around Sarajevo from the summer of 1992 through to the autumn of 1995 is that one side, the Bosnian Serb side, undeniably laid siege to the city of Sarajevo, which I remind you had been declared a safe area by the Security Council of the United Nations. Elsewhere in Bosnia that war took different aspects, depending on the region, and there were regions, as I mentioned earlier, for example, in the -- with respect to Bihac, where fighting in 1994 was set off by a Bosnian government defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I'm not asking you that. I'm asking you whether it is clear that this was a conflict between two sides, that it wasn't a one-sided attack by the Army of Republika Srpska. And as you have now explained that that was a security zone, is it logical, then, that no firing should come from a security area on the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I thought it was implicit when I acknowledged that it was a war, that a war necessitates two sides to a conflict. That, I acknowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. But do you assume, Mr. Williams, that had it not been for the opening of fire from Sarajevo against positions under the control of the VRS, would then have the Army of Republika Srpska opened fire on Sarajevo just like that, without any reason or provocation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have to say to you that on very many occasions, I would say the vast majority of occasions, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We must bring matters to a close today. Dr. Williams, we've received a message to the effect that you have to leave tomorrow morning. You have to get back to London. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to return to London, if I can, at midday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- I'm told 11.15 or 11.30, would that be right, for leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For leaving the Tribunal, yes, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, the position is this, that the accused has had one hour and a quarter. If he has an hour and a half tomorrow, that will be the same time as the Prosecution. We'll consider how long he should have. But, Mr. Milosevic, it won't be very much more than an hour and a half. And remember, a great deal of time is wasted when you argue with the witnesses to try and force them to agree to what you say, when their evidence is totally complicated -- to the contrary. And a great deal of time is spent in this case while you try and argue them into a position which is contrary to the one which they hold.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I understand your efforts to give me an equal amount of time, but I would request that you give me somewhat more time. Also, I hope that Mr. Williams will not deny that his answers are rather lengthy and that they take up a lot of time too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Almost as much as your questions. Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00. Would you be back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
